brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. The same page says "Xplor Technologies is the parent company of PerfectMind" and that Xplor "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe". One conflict is worth recording rather than resolving: nextrec.com says PerfectMind was founded in 1998, while Xplor's corporate site says "Founded in 1988, NextRec". Both are the family's own materials and they disagree; neither was treated as settled here.

brands.name: ePACT
brands.description:
ePACT Network sells emergency and health forms automation, described on its homepage as "Emergency and health forms automation that integrates seamlessly with rec management systems" and on its parks and recreation page as a way for "rec leaders to collect, manage and access health & emergency information, waivers and consent forms - all in one secure, compliant platform". The government function is narrow and specific: it is the participant-paperwork layer under a parks and recreation department's programs. The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

recdesk.com could not be read. Both the apex and www forms answer a plain fetch with an HTTP 202 and a Sucuri interstitial, and a real browser is served a "Robot Challenge Screen" that did not clear on repeated attempts. Xplor writes: "Founded in 2005, RecDesk provides scalable, easy-to-use software for parks and recreation departments, aquatic centers, schools, community centers, HOAs, and small municipalities. Its integrations with access control, GIS/address databases, and financial systems help teams streamline facility scheduling, program management, and operational workflows - reducing manual effort and system fragmentation." Xplor adds that "Business and community leaders can run more efficient programs, offer better resident experiences, and make data-driven decisions that strengthen their community services."

RecDesk is one of the four brands Xplor lists on its Xplor Recreation page, alongside Vermont Systems, NextRec and CampBrain, and Xplor's "Visit RecDesk" link points to recdesk.com. The distinction Xplor's own wording draws between the siblings is the size and type of buyer: RecDesk is described for "small municipalities", aquatic centers and HOAs, where Vermont Systems is described for "municipal, county, state, and federal military recreation organizations". RecDesk's postings run through the Rippling board shared across this family, clubessential-holdings-cjb, which also carries an asset named Xplor_Logo_withTag_Color.png. Beyond that, this record is deliberately short. Anything further about RecDesk's product, customers or scale would have to be invented, because its site refused to be read.

paragraphs: nextRec sells cloud based software for running parks and recreation departments, from program registration to facility rentals, with a self service side for residents. Buyers range from small villages to large counties and the government staff in between.

Staff set up single or recurring classes, courses, drop-ins, and programs, with conflict checking built in. The booking side covers indoor and outdoor facilities, parks, fields, campgrounds, meeting spaces, and party venues. Payments, memberships, and product sales run through the same system, online or on-site. Reports can be created, run, and exported in real time.

The same platform is marketed to K-12 schools and to higher education institutions. Associations use it so members can pay and manage their own accounts at any hour. The company says the platform complies with PCI, ISO, and SOC standards. Customers keep ownership of their data, which the site says stays in its country of origin. Support is offered 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

paragraphs: nextRec sells cloud based software for running parks and recreation departments, from program registration to facility rentals, with a self service side for residents. Buyers range from small villages to large counties and the government staff in between.

Staff set up single or recurring classes, courses, drop-ins, and programs, with conflict checking built in. The booking side covers indoor and outdoor facilities, parks, fields, campgrounds, meeting spaces, and party venues. The company says the platform complies with PCI, ISO, and SOC standards. Customers keep ownership of their data, which the site says stays in its country of origin. before.name: Agents of Discovery
before.description: Mobile augmented-reality game platform licensed to airports, parks and public agencies to engage visitors with location-triggered educational missions and wayfinding-style content.

paragraphs: Agents of Discovery turns physical spaces such as museums, airports, campuses, libraries, stadiums and entire cities into interactive learning environments by blending AI-driven content generation with place-based augmented reality gameplay. Customers become what the company calls Mission Makers, turning their own stories, spaces and content into augmented reality experiences.

Location-based challenges are placed on site and tied to the customer's own content, or played from anywhere. A site can also deploy a fully customized AI avatar as its on-site guide. Self-guided tours are offered around the clock. Exhibits can be built for aquariums, zoos and museums. Text-to-speech and multiple language options are meant to keep the platform reachable for players with diverse abilities and backgrounds.

Airports are one named setting, where the pitch is turning downtime into interactive adventures built for travelers. Junior Ranger Missions on the platform cover subjects from palaeontology and fossils to International Migratory Bird Day. The chief academic officer works with public and private organizations across the United States, Australia and Canada on visitor experience. The company describes itself as a Harvard-incubated AI and augmented reality company.

before.name: Amilia
before.description: SmartRec activity registration and facility management platform - exhibited at NRPA 2026

paragraphs: Amilia sells software that pulls memberships, program registration, payments, and reporting into one system. The customer it describes is the community organization that runs classes, memberships, and facilities for local families.

Registration happens through a branded online store that can stand on its own or sit inside the organization's existing website. Age or skill restrictions and defined registration periods control who can sign up for which activity. Waitlists fill open spots as soon as a registration is cancelled. On the facilities side, a calendar keeps bookings, activities, and rental contracts in sync so staff can see which space is in use and when. Access rules decide which memberships, activities, or passes open the door at each entry point.
The company states that over 1,500 organizations have chosen it. It advertises a 99.99% uptime guarantee for round-the-clock selling. Help is offered by live chat, phone, and email.

paragraphs: FMX sells facilities and maintenance management software that organizations use to streamline processes and get more out of their assets. For cities and counties, the pitch is maximizing asset performance, allocating spaces and funding, and streamlining resident service delivery. A school edition promises facility management software that will meet a district where it is at.

Work order management streamlines request submissions and helps staff resolve maintenance issues. Preventive maintenance handles compliance and schedules recurring tasks. Reporting tracks labor hours and costs so investments can be justified. Separate products cover vehicles, keeping a fleet on the road and tracking repairs. The products are cloud-based. A 14-day free trial is offered.

The company says it serves over 400K professionals. Beyond schools it sells into public works, covering public infrastructure, assets, public property, capital projects, and community events. It points to 400+ reviews on Capterra, Software Advice, and G2. Pricing turns on how many users an organization has, or the number of students enrolled for public K-12 schools.

paragraphs: OfferioRFP sells a secure, AI-powered platform that helps small and mid-sized businesses generate compliant and professional proposals. The platform works from documents a customer supplies, and the site tells users to upload past proposals and corporate documents so the tool follows an organization's own language. The pages state that the tool improves as a proposal library grows without exposing customer data to public AI models.

The work it covers is grouped on the page as government RFPs and tenders, grants and funding programs, and standing offers and RFQs. Customers use it to respond to municipal, provincial/state, federal, and agency RFPs with requirement analysis and compliance alignment. An assistant inside the product interprets requirements, drafts evaluator-ready responses, validates compliance, and surfaces supporting materials. A monitoring feature surfaces public-sector RFPs so a team spends its time on qualification rather than searching.

OfferioRFP runs on OfferioAI, which the page calls a purposefully built Business AI Engine. The site claims the platform saves on average 70% of time spent on custom proposal creations. A published set of questions says the product automates both RFP discovery and response generation using existing business documents.

before.name: GovStream.AI
before.description: AI permitting and land-use copilot: research assistant, guided applications, staff permit center ($3.6M seed; Bellevue, Louisville Metro)

paragraphs: Govstream.ai sells permitting software to cities and counties, aimed at the point where an applicant is trying to work out what their project actually requires. It is positioned as an addition to the systems a city already runs rather than a replacement for them.

A research assistant answers questions about a specific property, using zoning, overlays and GIS data so an applicant can see what applies to that parcel. An application assistant takes the plans first, pulls project details out of them and prefills the forms. A completeness score flags gaps before anything is submitted. Staff get a console that holds permit data, adopted codes, GIS layers, historical permits and conversations in one searchable place.

The company names Bellevue, Washington, as the site of its first pilot and reports that it cut inbound questions. Louisville is described as building an end-to-end workflow meant to stop incomplete applications before they are submitted. Everett is listed as another partner city. The site describes the product as SOC 2-ready and able to work with a city's existing infrastructure. Its press section links coverage of a seed round.

quote.text: Accessible housing starts with predictable permitting

provenance.quote: Turn permitting requirements into clear, personalized and parcel-specific guidance so applicants submit complete applications the first time.
Govstream.ai integrates with your GIS, codes, and review systems to reflect your policies and operations.
Guidance is tailored to each property using zoning, overlays, and GIS data, so applicants see what applies to their specific parcel.
Applicants upload plans first. Project details are extracted and forms are prefilled automatically.
A live completeness score flags gaps before submission.
Permit data, adopted codes, GIS layers, historical permits, and conversations connected in one searchable platform.

Govstream.ai is secure, SOC 2-ready, and works with your existing infrastructure.

before.name: Computronix
before.description: POSSE permitting, licensing and regulatory platform for state and local agencies - exhibited at ICC 2026

paragraphs: Computronix sells off-the-shelf software solutions for permitting, licensing, alcoholic beverage control, and gaming control. Those products run on POSSE, a web-based platform for automating permitting, licensing, enforcement and compliance workflows.

The permitting product automates workflows for building, planning, engineering, permitting, inspections and code enforcement. The alcoholic beverage control product manages the business and data behind liquor licensing, compliance and enforcement. The gaming product is aimed at agencies seeking a risk-based regulatory model for the gaming industry. The company says the software is engineered to comply with high security and regulatory compliance standards, including NIST, FedRAMP and ISO. Newer offerings include AI-powered portal assistance that helps applicants find answers and navigate permitting processes.

Computronix was founded in 1979 by Herman Leusink. It describes growing from a single employee to nearly two hundred employees and dozens of clients in major population centers across North America. One case study covers the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission, which regulates and controls that state's alcoholic beverage industry. The same alcohol system is used in nine other states and two provinces for alcohol industry regulation. Another case study describes the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario using POSSE ABC for liquor control, gaming, horse racing and recreational cannabis.

before.name: GovBuilt
before.description: Configurable permitting, licensing and workflow platform for local government

paragraphs: GovBuilt sells community development software to local government agencies, covering plan review, code enforcement, licensing and compliance in a single platform. On the site the product is presented under the MCCi name, with a claim that an agency can process permits up to 80% faster. The company also builds government websites that it describes as ADA-compliant and mobile-friendly.

Guided digital forms walk applicants through each requirement and flag missing information before submission. Applicants then get automatic status updates at every stage of the process. Inspectors complete reviews, log photos and update permit statuses from the job site. License records connect to supporting documents, inspection records, correspondence and approval history through a Laserfiche integration. As a license approaches expiration, automated renewal notices go out with what the business owner needs to finish online. For code enforcement, community members submit complaints and track case status through a public-facing portal. Officers document violations with photos and update case records directly from the property.

The company describes the platform as a browser-based SaaS product hosted on Microsoft Azure. An Android and iOS mobile application is offered for staff and inspectors. Agency staff are said to configure forms, requirements and workflows without submitting IT tickets or calling a vendor. A county planner in Pottawatomie County, KS is quoted saying permits that used to take 10 to 12 days now go out the same day in most cases.

before.name: Bitfocus
before.description: Clarity HMIS and homelessness response systems for counties and CoCs

paragraphs: Bitfocus builds Clarity Human Services, the case record system a community uses to coordinate housing and services for people who are homeless. The pitch is aimed at continuums of care that need to move people into housing and show funders what happened.

The system covers coordinated entry, case planning, and outreach work done in the field on a phone. It joins up records from across the continuum so agencies stop keeping separate copies of the same client. Reports can be generated against HUD, SOC, HIPAA and local standards, and access is scoped by role. There is a separate configuration for domestic violence providers, where client safety and privacy are treated differently.

Alongside the software the company sells services: system design, health evaluation, training, and taking over day-to-day administration of the system. Bitfocus describes itself as founder-led and says it talks regularly with HUD, USICH, NAEH and Community Solutions.

paragraphs: OpenCounter sells permit discovery software that answers applicants' questions before they reach City Hall. The platform tells applicants where a project is allowed, which permits it needs and how much they cost, without asking city staff. Pricing depends on the population size of a jurisdiction and the number of portals procured.

The Business Portal is aimed at entrepreneurs working out the costs and requirements of starting a business. A use code search lets applicants enter simple terms rather than code language. Zoning maps show where a project is permitted, conditionally permitted, or prohibited in the jurisdiction. Fees are calculated as applicants enter project details, and a summary page lists required permits by department or in the order to apply.

The Residential Portal applies the same permit discovery to home improvement projects. The Special Events Portal handles event permitting from discovery through issuance, with applicants paying online and downloading permits after approval. Configuration and implementation are done by the company, which asks the jurisdiction for data such as ArcGIS shapefiles, a permit catalog and overlay districts. Zoning and municipal code updates are made for the duration of a subscription at no charge.

quote.text: OpenCounter helps applicants answer pre-application questions without calls, emails, or visits to City Hall, while streamlining staff processes for increased efficiency.

provenance.quote: Answer applicants’ permitting questions before they get to City Hall.
Applicants learn where their project is allowed, which permits they need, and how much they cost, without even having to ask city staff.
Costs will vary depending on the population size of your jurisdiction and the number of portals you procure.
Help entrepreneurs understand the costs and requirements of starting a business.

OpenCounter takes care of everything from permit discovery to issuance within the portal. Applicants simply complete their applications and pay online, then download their permits and receipts after their applications have been approved.
OpenCounter will perform 99 percent of the work involved in configuration and implementation.
We'll handle all of your zoning and municipal code updates for the duration of your OpenCounter subscription, completely free of charge.

before.name: Cloudpermit
before.description: Cloud e-permitting and community development software for ~500 local governments (Finnish-born) - exhibited at ICC 2026

paragraphs: Cloudpermit sells online public works and community development software meant to help local governments modernize. The promise is a system that is easier for staff and better for residents.

Building permit applications come in online and permits can be issued as soon as payment is processed. Land use review covers rezonings, variances, subdivisions, site plans and public hearings. Code compliance ties complaint management, inspections and case tracking together. On the licensing side staff issue, revoke and renew licenses. The same pages cover short-term rental compliance. Inspections run in an app that works whether the inspector is online or offline. Interactive maps tie into a jurisdiction's own GIS.

Staff and residents can work in English, Spanish and French. Cloudpermit says the software is built in collaboration with local authorities and evolves alongside the governments it serves. It claims permits and licenses are issued 80% faster than on paper. An AI assistant called NoVa is offered inside the citizen portal.

paragraphs: OpenGov sells a cloud platform for cities, counties, and state agencies that connects budgeting, finance, permitting, and asset management in one system. The Public Service Platform brings ERP and Community Operations products together, spanning Financial Management, Budgeting & Performance, Procurement & Contract Management, Permitting & Licensing, 311 Request Management, Utility Billing, and Payroll. OG Assist is the AI assistant built into every product, helping staff find answers, draft documents, and complete guided actions across the platform.

Software is built specifically for cities, counties, and state agencies, and the pages say over 2,000 governments run day-to-day operations on it. The buyers named are cities, counties, townships, special districts, school districts, utilities, and state agencies across the United States. Compliance controls built in cover GASB, FEMA, HUD, ARPA, and FLSA, and the platform is stated to be SOC 2 compliant.

OpenGov states 4,500+ government software implementations completed, with timelines that vary by product and organizational complexity, typically ranging from 3 to 6 months. Government App Builder is a no-code platform that lets IT teams build custom forms, workflows, and citizen-facing apps, with permissions, audit logs, and version history.

paragraphs: Archistar sells AI plan review software to local governments, with a product called AI PreCheck that speeds building code and zoning compliance checks so permits can be issued faster. The same platform is offered to developers, architects and certifiers, who can check compliance before submitting to a municipality or council.

Submitters drag and drop design files onto the platform, which accepts PDF, CAD or BIM formats and reviews them in 2D or 3D. The software then evaluates each submission against the city's local codes and regulations. It is built on generative AI, computer vision and machine learning. Applicants receive standardized reports. For municipalities and councils with particular zoning, planning and compliance requirements, tailored and white-labeled versions are offered.

The company says Archistar was founded by Dr. Benjamin Coorey in 2010 and began life as an education portal. It grew from a university research project into a platform that could read planning rules, run feasibility tests and generate compliant designs in minutes. The site states that Archistar powers digital planning for over 30 cities and governments across Australia, Canada and the United States. Among the municipalities it names supporting are LA County, the City of Los Angeles, the City of Austin and the City of New York. Offices are listed across Los Angeles, Vancouver and Sydney.

paragraphs: Civica makes software that public bodies use to deliver critical services to citizens around the world. It says over 6,000 public bodies use that software to help provide critical services to over 100 million citizens.

Its solutions span local and central government, health and community care, housing and social care, libraries and education, and regulatory and compliance services. The company describes integrated cloud platforms that automate workflows, support data-driven decision-making and reduce operational costs. Named products include Spydus, a library management system. Civica also sells master data management for state and local government. It says it is an approved supplier on major government frameworks.

Civica was established in 2001 and describes itself as one of the UK's largest software companies. Its team has grown to 5,500 colleagues, one-third of whom have worked in the sectors it serves. Acquisitions are part of the strategy, with more than 37 completed in the last 10 years. The company reports delivery in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, India, North America and Europe. Customer stories on its site include delivering a single citizen view for the State of Alaska.

before.name: Placemetry
before.description: AI street-imagery analysis: pavement condition, sign inventory, and blight for public works and code enforcement - exhibited at Smart Cities Connect 2026

paragraphs: Placemetry drives a city and captures photos from the public right-of-way, then analyzes properties and roadways with AI so departments can get ahead of problems rather than react to them. Each vehicle is equipped with three high-resolution cameras, one facing forward and one facing to each side, capturing street-level imagery in a single drive. Forward-facing cameras deliver per-segment pavement condition, an asset inventory, and safety screening in a single pass.

Side cameras capture a wide view of the public right-of-way in one pass, including properties, yards, sidewalks, trees, and vegetation. The same dataset feeds Code Enforcement, Economic Development, and Forestry & Parks. All imagery is captured from the public right-of-way, faces and license plates are blurred, and the city owns the data.

One cadence is a single citywide survey with no subscription required. Another is a quarterly or bi-annual citywide sweep in which Placemetry teams drive every street and the AI scores properties. A third option puts cameras on city vehicles the city already operates, so garbage trucks and street sweepers capture passive citywide coverage. Delivery runs through direct API integrations, standard spreadsheet downloads, or a secure web app, with REST API Endpoints and Webhooks.

quote.text: If you can see it from the street, we can measure it.

paragraphs: Camino sells permitting and licensing software to government agencies. The system is meant for building, planning, business and event applications. A companion product, now called the Clariti Guide, works alongside software an agency already has to help applicants better understand the process.

Each application type is configured with a tailored workflow that keeps every step in order. Staff conduct digital plan review in the system and track multiple review cycles. Applicants can request or schedule inspections online. The Guide checks automatically whether a business or construction process is allowed based on the zone, and identifies extra approvals that may be required. It also estimates the fees owed for a project and how long approval might take.

Camino is now a Clariti brand. The permitting and licensing system it sold under its own name is now called Clariti Launch. Among the results listed on the site is a 70% decrease in the length of permit counter visits. Another says a permit portal was live one month after starting with Camino.

before.name: GeoCivix
before.description: Cloud permitting, plan review, inspections, and code enforcement for local gov and fire districts - exhibited at ICC 2026

paragraphs: GeoCivix sells cloud-based software that cities, counties and municipalities use to run permitting, licensing, inspections, plan review and citizen services from one system. The pitch is a replacement for paper-based workflows with digital applications, automated routing, electronic plan review, mobile inspections and online payments.

Applicants use a government portal open around the clock, where they manage their projects and pay fees without calling or coming into the office. Staff mark up documents and let the system automate routing. Notifications and comment letters go back out to applicants as reviews move along. Inspectors work from a tablet or smart phone in the field, taking photos, creating reports and managing workloads on site. Permits, inspections, plans, documents, notes and approvals stay organized in one place.

Staff, reviewers, inspectors, citizens and contractors all work from the same project record. An implementation team starts by collecting application forms, communication templates, fee formulas and document workflows for configuration. The company says many agencies launch initial workflows in as little as 6 weeks, with full deployment typically completed within a few months. Every subscription is said to include unlimited technical support for all users. Listed integrations include ESRI ArcGIS, Bluebeam Revu, Cityworks, Infor/Hansen, FireRMS, Laserfiche and payment systems.

paragraphs: City Detect sells a camera and software service that helps municipalities and counties find and address urban blight before complaints pile up. Cameras ride on a city's existing fleet vehicles and collect images of properties as those vehicles drive their normal routes. The company's PASS AI then detects and maps signs of urban blight and decay from the public right of way.

Roof-mounted data collection units capture street-level imagery during routine city operations. Once the images are processed, each detection is assigned a severity score from 1 to 4 and placed on an interactive map. The conditions it picks up run to illegal dumping, tire accumulations, snipe signs, and graffiti. Staff can export timestamped, image-backed reports in a few clicks.

The company says it was founded in 2021. One published case study describes Cathedral City partnering with City Detect in June 2025. For each municipality the company performs local calibration meant to cut false-positive detections and match local rules.

paragraphs: MuniLogic sells municipal management software to local governments in the United States. Its main product, MuniLogic CE+, is municipal management software for small to mid-sized local governments, built from integrated modules. before.name: Social Explorer
before.description: Demographic data, mapping, and visualization with 500K+ variables for gov, academia, and planning

paragraphs: Social Explorer sells a subscription web application for community analysis, built so that data is acquired and processed before the customer arrives. The application couples a data library with an AI-enabled Data Navigator that takes natural-language questions and returns dataset-specific analysis. Output takes the form of maps, charts, tables, and reports, and data can be exported to Excel, CSV, PDF, PNG, SAS, or SPSS formats.

The mapping product, SE Research, covers location-based community data at every geographic level and is positioned for users without a data science background. A subscription includes a library of crime, demographic, economic, environmental, equity, health, housing, political, and transportation data drawn from public and private sources.

SE Transform, a data pipeline management product, launches as a managed service and is built on Apache Airflow infrastructure. SE AI is sold as a domain-specific data chat interface, with a conversational front end, an API layer, and an admin panel. The homepage says the customer base includes educational and research institutions, government agencies, non-profits, healthcare systems, and businesses.

quote.text: Most of the time spent on community analysis involves acquiring and processing data.

Our demographic mapping software is designed to make demographic data accessible to everyone who wants to be data-driven.

before.name: Citizenserve
before.description: Cloud permitting, licensing and code enforcement software for small and mid-size municipalities

paragraphs: Citizenserve sells cloud software for community development, pulling permitting, inspections, code enforcement, planning and zoning, and licensing into a single system. Its buyers range from small towns and growing cities to large counties, departments inside major cities, and specialized agencies.

The company says the platform matches an agency's existing workflows without custom coding. It connects to GIS and financial systems among others. Applications, processing, and tracking sit in one secure system that the company says runs at 99.999% uptime. The licensing side covers online applications, automated renewals, payments, contractor tracking, and compliance. A published case describes work with Lawrence, Massachusetts to create a dedicated food permit type and a custom food establishment inspection form. On completion, the system generates an inspection report formatted for state submission.

The company says many of its clients have stayed with it for over twenty years. It reports that 99% of users give its support team a thumbs up. It also claims 99.999% uptime and zero data losses over more than 20 years.

paragraphs: Bitco Software sells PermitTrax, hosted software for governments and agencies. It follows a permit from application through to final inspection.

Building permits are accepted and issued online, with mobile inspections carried out in the field. A planning module circulates applications, keeps up communication with applicants, and issues land use permits. A licensing module renews and issues business licenses and takes payments online or over the counter. Code enforcement staff track complaint cases, run in-field inspections, and issue violation letters and notices. A public portal called Citizens Connect lets residents track permit progress, request inspections, upload files, apply for permits, and pay online. Inspectors work from a companion application on an Apple iPad.

The company was established in December 2002. Cory Jorgensen is listed as founder and president. The suite is now described as a land management system covering permit, license, and code case tracking, reporting, GIS integration, and electronic plan review. Pricing is a flat fee for the license and maintenance. That fee is said to cover implementation, data conversion, training, and unlimited users.

before.name: CityView
before.description: Community development, permitting and inspections software for municipalities

paragraphs: CityView sells community development software to municipalities, giving them one integrated system for permitting, inspections, planning, code enforcement and licensing. The company describes the platform as purpose-built for local government.

Permits run their full lifecycle in one system, with electronic plans review, mobile field access and automated workflows configured to a jurisdiction's own rules rather than a generic template. Planning teams track rezoning, subdivision, variance and development applications through review, referral and public hearing. Complaints and enforcement cases connect to the same permits and property data. Licensing covers business licenses, cannabis permits, short-term rentals and animal licenses, with online applications, automated renewals and fee calculation. Residents and contractors submit applications, schedule inspections and pay online at any hour.

The company has focused on software for local governments since 1982. It calls that platform one of the first community development and permitting software platforms in North America. The about page says the business was founded by former local government employees for local government. CityView is part of Harris Computer Systems and Constellation Software Inc. One customer story describes the Town of Bradford West Gwillimbury, Ontario, moving to a fully electronic plan review process while upgrading its CityView technology.

before.name: Gridics
before.description: Zoning code automation and development capacity analysis for cities

paragraphs: Gridics converts municipal zoning code text into parcel-level data that people can look at visually. The work is aimed at two audiences, developers choosing sites and cities trying to make their zoning easier to understand.

A patented zoning rules engine processes the data and powers the applications. Underneath it sits a mix of public property data, GIS shapes, and transit data. CodeHUB handles code publishing, letting staff collaborate on, manage, and publish zoning code changes. ZoneCheck is offered as a way to virtualize the zoning and planning front counter. ZoneIQ analyzes development potential and capacity scenarios in real-time 3D.

In Miami, the company built and implemented CodeHUB with the city's planning and zoning departments. It reports that over 60,000 users a year visit that instance for zoning information. For a study commissioned by the Wynwood Business Improvement District, the team modeled over 200,000,000 gsf of maximum buildable area across two proposed transit sites. The company says a city's code text can be digitized in as little as four weeks.

before.name: CaseWorthy
before.description: Case management and HMIS for government-funded human services programs

paragraphs: CaseWorthy sells a software platform for case and program management in human services. Its buyers are nonprofit organizations and local and state governments that deliver social care programs.

The platform pulls programs, people, data and workflows together in one system rather than scattering them across separate tools. Agencies configure their own workflows, forms, assessments and service plans to match how each program operates. Reporting for funders is built into the platform instead of assembled in spreadsheets. Underneath sits a data lakehouse called CORE that consolidates information from CaseWorthy applications and outside sources. CORE ships baseline data models for particular sectors, including HMIS for homeless services, aging services and workforce development metrics.

Beyond case management there are applications for HCBS and I/DD providers covering care coordination, scheduling and Medicaid-supported service delivery. Another handles scheduling, documentation and billing for Home and Community-Based Services agencies. An AI copilot named Cara is embedded in the platform to reduce documentation time and surface insights. The company states that the organizations it serves touch more than 41% of the US population.

before.name: Azora Software
before.description: Short-term rental compliance: finds unpermitted rentals, automates permitting and tax enforcement - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026

paragraphs: Azora Software sells short-term rental compliance software to local governments. The problem it targets is that ordinary permitting systems only capture the rentals that volunteer to apply, leaving the rest unseen.

To close that gap the platform aggregates data from more than 75 sources, cross-references listings against property and parcel records, compiles verifiable evidence and connects to a city's code enforcement operations. Permitting then runs against that discovered address list, covering applications, renewals, status tracking and enforcement actions. Separate tools handle transaction reporting and statement reconciliation to support tax auditing and remittance. For enforcement and appeals, the platform generates PDFs and consolidated evidence of rental activity on demand.

Cities are the customer, and other government technology vendors also bring Azora in for short-term rental work beside the platforms those cities already run. The company says it was founded by three experienced professionals with complementary expertise and runs on a lean structure. One of them is a former city manager of Garden City, Utah. The same team previously built STR Helper, which the about page says was acquired by Host Compliance in 2019. Each customer keeps a named project manager who moves from launch into ongoing support.

before.name: GovWell
before.description: AI permitting and licensing platform: 24/7 resident assistant, AI code-compliance review - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026, Maryland Municipal League 2026, ICC 2026
before.source: ICMA 2025; NACo 2026; ICMA 2026; NLC City Summit 2026; Maryland Municipal League 2026; ICC 2026

paragraphs: GovWell sells software that city and county governments use to run permitting, licensing, planning, and code enforcement work. Residents and businesses use the same system to reach services, pay, and get answers outside office hours.

Permits, plan review, and inspections are handled together in one place for staff. Licensing runs online too, with applicants filing, paying, and renewing while staff keep records and approvals on their side. Code enforcement officers track cases, schedule inspections, and follow issues to closure. The company argues that AI can do real work in these processes, reviewing applications against local code, answering resident questions, flagging violations in plans, and routing inspections.

GovWell says it was founded by the son of a general contractor who watched his father struggle to get permits quickly. Its case for existing is that local governments cannot hire software engineers at competitive salaries. Deployment strategists and configuration tooling are meant to shorten implementations against older systems.

paragraphs: SwiftGov is presented as an AI-native operating system for local government, built to strengthen permit and plan review, compliance, knowledge, data, and service delivery. The platform automates intake processing, flags potential code conflicts before they become resubmittals, and standardizes reviewer comments. The products listed for the Hernando County engagement are SwiftGov, Development Services Transformation, GIS Services, and Swift Analytics.

The jurisdictions named on the SwiftGov page are Hernando County, Pasco County, Clay County, Walton County, City of Jacksonville, City of Titusville, and Hernando County Clerk of Court, all in Florida. The case studies page describes municipal development services teams using SwiftGov for regulatory review. The case study ties the deployment to the rebuild surge after Hurricane Helene and Hurricane Milton in 2024.

Initial plan review time at Hernando County is reported as 30 days to 15 minutes, a 93% reduction in single-family home zoning review times. The county estimates direct net savings of $1.5 million annually across four primary areas, including reduced reliance on temporary staff and third-party plan review.

paragraphs: GovSense sells cloud software for local governments, built on Oracle NetSuite. The suite spans finance and accounting, budgeting, utility billing, fund and project management, economic development, asset management, GIS, inspections and enforcement, planning, and permitting and licensing.

A jurisdiction can buy the whole thing at once or add one module at a time. Because every department works in the same system, the company says there is a single version of the truth to rely on. Staff are meant to reach that information securely from any device, at any time. The multi-tenancy of a true-cloud product is presented as removing reliance on in-house IT. Implementation is described as driven by business processes rather than by technology. The company says it tailors the software to a jurisdiction's requirements and delivers in weeks and months, not months and years.

GovSense describes itself as having built the first unified, true-cloud solution designed specifically for local government. The site claims over 40 years of experience behind the company. It also states that it was named a GovTech 100 company for a fifth consecutive year.

paragraphs: Clariti sells community development software to local governments, pitched at any size and budget. One edition is permitting software for large local governments. A second, Launch, is aimed at small to mid-sized local governments. A third product, CivCheck, uses AI to guide applicants toward a complete and compliant submission and staff through every check.

The software keeps the permit counter online, where applicants apply, pay, and track status. It also tracks code violations from report to resolution, with automatic case assignment and links to local zoning and codes. Staff can build a report, adjust a page layout, or create a new permit type themselves. The large-jurisdiction edition runs on the Salesforce Platform, whose APIs let a government connect its other tools. Launch customers can copy a peer's permitting workflows using a cloning tool. On the AI side, staff have to approve every interpretation the software makes.

The company says the large-jurisdiction product was built with input from government customers over 16 years. Its home page names Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Orange County among the cities and counties using Clariti. Launch pricing is stated as based on population rather than user count.

paragraphs: Euna Grants is grant management software that carries public funding work from discovery through closeout. The line is sold in three named parts, described on the page as Grants Research Software, Grant Seeking Software, and Grant Making Software. Research finds funding opportunities, seeking tracks tasks and deadlines through configurable workflows, and making covers application design, scoring, and award.

Listed capabilities include a research database of federal, state, municipal, local, and foundation funding opportunities, automatic deadline reminders, custom applications with field-level scoring criteria, and a reporting engine that pulls data from all fields in the system. Compliance and audit are stated as a focus, with audit trails described as FOIA-ready and public transparency tools listed as built in. Integration with a customer ERP is named as a way to move financial information.

Named customers on that page include Mariposa County, CA, a statewide grant administrator in Arizona, and the California Department of Housing & Community Development. A frequently asked questions entry lists public sector agencies, nonprofits, educational institutions, and any organization that manages grants.

before.name: Symbium
before.description: Instant automated permitting and zoning compliance checks for building departments

paragraphs: Symbium runs an instant permitting service that lets homeowners and contractors see what a property allows, scope a project such as solar panels or a heat pump, and then file and manage the permit application. The company is based in San Francisco and puts its initial focus on permitting for residential decarbonization projects.

Compliance checks run against the applicable building, zoning, and energy codes while the applicant is still scoping the work. The technology underneath, called Complaw, is described as a TurboTax-like mechanization of regulatory analysis first built by the founding team at Stanford AI Lab. It layers onto the permitting workflows a building department already has, with contractors getting issuance within seconds of applying.

Contractors use it to accelerate permit issuance across a range of project types. The company says it has saved contractors and city staff time, and puts the running total at 3,500,000 project hours so far. It names Elemental Impact, Third Derivative, Uptake Alliance, and IMPEL among its backers. It was founded by Leila Banijamali, Abhijeet Mohapatra and Michael Genesereth during work at Stanford University. Recognition it lists includes a California Building Officials industry achievement award and a United States Conference of Mayors Civic Challenge.

paragraphs: Accela sells software that government agencies use to run permitting, licensing, and asset management from a single system. Its applications are built for individual government service workflows and can operate together or be deployed only where an agency needs them.

For building departments, intake, plan review, inspections, and permit issuance sit in one workflow rather than in separate disconnected steps. Reviewers from different departments work the same record at once, with annotations and approvals tracked as they happen. Planning teams get the same shared review model, plus automated public notice generation, hearing schedules, and agency notifications. Applicants can see where a case stands and receive consolidated feedback from every reviewing department.

The company says it has thirty years of government expertise built into the product. Testimonials on the site are attributed to municipal staff, including a chief building official in McAllen, Texas. Residents and businesses who encounter Accela through a local agency are directed to that agency rather than to the company.

paragraphs: Objective Corporation sells software meant to help government shift to being completely digital. It says thousands of public sector organizations use its software for developing policies with impact and accelerating processes. One of its stated aims is to streamline the building assessment and consent process.

Objective Trapeze is electronic plan review software that helps planning and building departments review plans quickly and accurately while checking compliance with ICC codes and amendments. Stamping is digital, and a 100-page application can be stamped in a few mouse clicks, with the software finding white space to place the stamp. Objective Connect is an IRAP assessed external file sharing product that gives control over information shared outside a council. Objective RegWorks centralises, tracks and administers the compliance process, including education and engagement. A separate product keeps disclosure document management production, review, verification and publication in one central system.

The company states that more than 500 local governments in the UK, Australia and New Zealand rely on Objective Trapeze to conduct plan reviews faster. It puts the file sharing product at more than 200 organisations worldwide.

roles.title: Business Development & Senior Key Account Manager – Paris, petite-couronne and Private Parking Operators

paragraphs: Arrive sells urban mobility technology to city governments, parking operators and businesses. On the parking side that means demand insight and digital payments for parking and EV charging.

Drivers start, stop, extend and pay for a session from an app. Operators run payment stations and in-car integrations from the same platform. License plate recognition can start and end sessions automatically as cars enter and leave. The company says its EV solutions connect with more than 400 charge point operators. For city planners, dashboards report parking use, traffic trends and mobility patterns to guide planning.

Arrive describes itself as a coming together of Flowbird Group, EasyPark Group, Parkopedia and others. The about page dates the story back to 1955. That timeline opens with Cale installing its first parking meters. Within the group, Flowbird is described as delivering mobility solutions in over 6,000 cities across 80 countries. EasyPark is described as present in over 4,000 cities across more than 20 countries.

quote.text: Arrive empowers operators, decision-makers, and businesses to make smarter urban mobility choices

provenance.quote: Arrive empowers operators, decision-makers, and businesses to make smarter urban mobility choices
We help you understand demand, optimize space, and reduce traffic with data-driven insights and digital payments for parking and EV charging
Let drivers start, stop, extend, and pay for parking with an app.
Arrive’s smart payment stations, mobile solutions, and in-car integration give you greater control and operational insight.
License Plate Recognition (LPR) technology automatically starts and ends parking sessions as drivers enter and exit simply by scanning their license plate.
Our EV solutions work with 400+ charge point operators.
Clear dashboards give you visibility over your city’s parking, traffic trends, and mobility use for smarter planning
Flowbird Group, EasyPark Group, Parkopedia, and many others, have each helped shape how people move through cities.
Shaping smart cities since 1955
Cale installs their first parking meters.
Flowbird delivers mobility solutions in over 6,000 cities across 80 countries
Present in over 4,000 cities across more than 20 countries, EasyPark simplifies parking, charging and mobility worldwide.

profile.description:
Arrive is the Stockholm-based parent company of a group of parking, payment and public-transport brands. Its site footer gives the address "Birger Jarlsgatan 57B, 113 56 Stockholm". Its own release of June 12, 2025 says the name Arrive "will replace EasyPark Group and Flowbird Group" and that it "will be the overarching parent company" for EasyPark, Flowbird, ParkMobile, Parkopedia, RingGo, Yellowbrick, Your Parking Space and other brands. The same release says the consumer brands and apps "will remain unaffected for the foreseeable future". The release boilerplate describes the company as "Present in over 90 countries and 20,000 cities".

The home page sorts the offer into five groups: parking ("digital payments for parking and EV charging"), city planning (mobility data), public transport ("our open payment solution and smart ticketing devices"), fleets and businesses, and in-car services for automakers. Public buyers appear on the solution pages. The public-transport page says "We help operators and local governments simplify ticketing" and lists Open Payment, railway-certified ticket validators, bus driver consoles and vending machines. The city-planner page offers dashboards "for decision-makers" with "policy-grade insights". The parking-operators page lists payment stations, mobile paid parking and in-car payment. Case studies on the home page cover Las Vegas pay stations, a parking app in downtown Detroit, Monaco's MaaS app and Lerici, Italy.

The about page lists the family: EasyPark, Flowbird, RingGo, ParkMobile, Yellowbrick, Parkopedia, YourParkingSpace and Parkimeter. It also has a timeline that starts with Cale's first parking meters in Sweden in 1955 and ends with "2025 Arrive is launched". The leadership page names Cameron Clayton as chief executive and Niklas Savander as board chair. It also says "Arrive is backed by three investment firms: Verdane, Vitruvian Partners, and Searchlight Capital."

The footer Careers link goes to careers.arrive.com and the header Career link to jobs.ashbyhq.com/arrive. Press goes to [address removed], with a named contact for North America.

The Arrive Magazine PDF was not read. arrive.com/about returns 404; the real about page is /en/about/about-us. The headline counters on the home and about pages printed as "0", so no figures were taken from them.

brands.name: EasyPark (formerly EasyPark Group)
brands.description:
EasyPark Group is the old corporate name of the company now called Arrive. Arrive's June 12, 2025 release says EasyPark Group "unveiled a new name and identity" and that Arrive "will replace EasyPark Group and Flowbird Group". The old corporate site no longer works on its own. easyparkgroup.com forwards to www.easypark.com/en, which returned HTTP 404 when read. easyparkgroup.com/news/ forwards to the Arrive newsroom. One leftover is still live: careers.easyparkgroup.com loads under the title "Together, we make cities more livable! - EasyPark Group".

History from Arrive's about-page timeline: EasyPark was founded in Norway and Denmark in 2000-2001. "Mint acquires Payway and merges with EasyPark" in 2004-2005. EasyPark bought Telepark in Italy in 2014. In 2021 it acquired "Park Now Group, including RingGo and ParkMobile brands, and Parkimeter". It bought MPLA (Czech Republic) and Handyparken (Austria) in 2024, then Flowbird and Parkopedia in 2025. Flowbird's November 2023 release says EasyPark Group "owns and develops the apps EasyPark, ParkMobile, RingGo and Park-line" and operates "in over 4,000 cities across more than 20 countries".

The EasyPark brand still runs its own site at easypark.com. From here it served a Dutch page (/nl) and an English page for Sweden (/en-se). It sells a consumer parking app ("the No.1 parking app in Europe") with pay-by-minute parking, EV charging and in-car parking. For public buyers, its "Cities and operators" page describes "a digital ecosystem where municipal authorities, private garage operators, and drivers, play a part in optimizing the available parking inventory". The services it lists are EasyPark Insights, The Parking Dashboard, EasyPark SmartHUB, Express pay, Digital Permits and EV charging. The page claims "4,400 +" cities and "7,700 +" parking operators. The site footer links "About Arrive" to arrive.com. Arrive's about page calls EasyPark "the leading provider of smart parking and mobility solutions in Europe".

For the board: the corporate body is now Arrive, and EasyPark is its European parking-app brand. No US public buyers appeared on the EasyPark pages read. Arrive's North American app is ParkMobile.

Not read: easyparkgroup.com itself (redirect ends in a 404), easypark.com/en and /en-gb (both 404), and the English "About EasyPark" page beyond a skim.

brands.name: Flowbird
brands.description:
Flowbird makes parking and public-transport payment hardware and software. flowbird.group now forwards to www.flowbird.com. Its home page carries the banner "EasyPark Group and Flowbird are now Arrive", which links to arrive.com.

Parking: the on-street page lists pay-and-display terminals and kiosks, including the Strada EVOL GEN 3, Strada TPAL GEN 3, Strada S5 GEN 3, StreetSmart S5 GEN 3, Compact S5 and Access S5. Across the range they take coins, cards, banknotes or city cards depending on the model (the Access S5 is cashless), on solar or mains power. The menu also lists off-street, EV charging, mobile and "Parking business services". Transport: the menu lists Equipment, Open Payment, MaaS and a "Transport Fare Collection Platform". The transport page says Flowbird aims to "optimize investment value for transport authorities and operators". It also lists account-based ticketing, Open Payment and back-office systems. Energy services are sold as Park&Gaz.

The about page claims "6000 Cities" and "Over 80 Countries", and says "84% of the 50 biggest cities in the world rely on Flowbird". Its history starts in 1968 with "The first parking meter is installed on the Paris streets". In 2003 Parkeon was created from Schlumberger's parking and ticketing division. In 2018 "Parkeon and Cale merge to become Flowbird". Since 2020 it has bought Yellowbrick (NL), YourParkingSpace (UK) and Piconet (RO).

US public buyers in its news list include "SEPTA Partners with Flowbird to Launch Advanced Commuter Parking System" (Sept 2024) and "Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) Partners with Flowbird to Modernize Transit System" (Sept 2024). Others are Pittsburgh Regional Transit (Aug 2024), "Flowbird Pay-by-Plate Pay Stations Launch in the City of New York" (June 2024), and Beverly Hills, Charleston SC, Clearwater FL, Rochester and Leavenworth.

Place in Arrive: Flowbird Group announced on November 9, 2023 its decision to be acquired by EasyPark Group, and EasyPark Group closed the purchase on January 15, 2025. Flowbird CEO Frédéric Beylier then left, and Cameron Clayton became CEO of the joint company. Arrive's about page describes Flowbird as delivering "mobility solutions in over 6,000 cities across 80 countries". Arrive's public-transport page sells open payment, validators and bus consoles but does not name Flowbird on that page.

Not read: the Equipment, Open Payment, MaaS and Fare Collection sub-pages. Also unread are Flowbird's own releases on the Yellowbrick, YourParkingSpace and Piconet purchases. The flowbird.com footer still reads "© Flowbird Group 2024", and the newest news item seen is dated May 19, 2025.

brands.name: ParkMobile
brands.description:
ParkMobile, LLC runs a US parking app and the parking-management tools behind it. Its about page says "in 2008, ParkMobile launched" and that drivers can "pay for street and garage parking without having to use a meter or kiosk". It also sells reservations for events, airports and campuses. The footer reads "© 2026 ParkMobile, LLC", and some of its releases carry Atlanta, GA datelines.

Public buyers: the provider menu has "ParkMobile for" pages for Municipalities, Event venues, Private operators, College campuses, and Transit and airports. The municipalities page says "Serving over 600 municipalities". It promises congestion control, flexible payment, links to existing parking hardware and software, analytics and more revenue, and offers a Dashboard product. The transit and airports page sells reservations and multi-location management to "transit operators". City customers named in its own news include:
- the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency (Nov 5, 2025), for "the city's 26,000 on-street parking spaces"
- Buffalo, NY (July 2025), including ParkMobile Insights analytics for the city
- the City of Tacoma (Aug 2026)
- Royal Oak, MI (Jan 2026)
- the Miami Parking Authority
- Durham, NC

Place in Arrive: its 2021 release says it "has been part of BMW and Daimler's mobility joint venture PARK NOW Group since March 2019". On June 1, 2021, EasyPark Group "announced today the completed acquisition of PARK NOW Group, including North American-based ParkMobile". At that point ParkMobile had "25 million users and a presence in over 450 cities". Its current releases call it part of Arrive. The Tacoma release opens "Part of the larger leading global mobility platform Arrive, ParkMobile offers drivers..." and the SFMTA release calls it "part of the global mobility company Arrive". Arrive staff speak for it: Scott Booker, "General Manager of Parking at Arrive", and Benoit Reliquet, Arrive's Head of Parking for North America. Its Careers link goes to careers.arrive.com, and its press contact is [address removed]. Arrive's about page lists it as "the leading provider of smart parking and mobility solutions in North America", "available in over 700 cities".

Not read: the later pages of the newsroom (only page 1 of 30 was listed) and the provider solution pages (Payments, Management, Insights).

why: owner 2026-10-20 'acquisitions?': Arrive's own ownership, read off its leadership page; the note the fold inherited from Flowbird described Flowbird being bought, not Arrive

EasyPark Group is the old corporate name of the company now called Arrive. Arrive's June 12, 2025 release says EasyPark Group "unveiled a new name and identity" and that Arrive "will replace EasyPark Group and Flowbird Group". The old corporate site no longer works on its own. easyparkgroup.com forwards to www.easypark.com/en, which returned HTTP 404 when read. easyparkgroup.com/news/ forwards to the Arrive newsroom. One leftover is still live: careers.easyparkgroup.com loads under the title "Together, we make cities more livable! - EasyPark Group".

History from Arrive's about-page timeline: EasyPark was founded in Norway and Denmark in 2000-2001. "Mint acquires Payway and merges with EasyPark" in 2004-2005. EasyPark bought Telepark in Italy in 2014. In 2021 it acquired "Park Now Group, including RingGo and ParkMobile brands, and Parkimeter". It bought MPLA (Czech Republic) and Handyparken (Austria) in 2024, then Flowbird and Parkopedia in 2025. Flowbird's November 2023 release says EasyPark Group "owns and develops the apps EasyPark, ParkMobile, RingGo and Park-line" and operates "in over 4,000 cities across more than 20 countries".

The EasyPark brand still runs its own site at easypark.com. From here it served a Dutch page (/nl) and an English page for Sweden (/en-se). It sells a consumer parking app ("the No.1 parking app in Europe") with pay-by-minute parking, EV charging and in-car parking. For public buyers, its "Cities and operators" page describes "a digital ecosystem where municipal authorities, private garage operators, and drivers, play a part in optimizing the available parking inventory". The services it lists are EasyPark Insights, The Parking Dashboard, EasyPark SmartHUB, Express pay, Digital Permits and EV charging. The page claims "4,400 +" cities and "7,700 +" parking operators. The site footer links "About Arrive" to arrive.com. Arrive's about page calls EasyPark "the leading provider of smart parking and mobility solutions in Europe".

For the board: the corporate body is now Arrive, and EasyPark is its European parking-app brand. No US public buyers appeared on the EasyPark pages read. Arrive's North American app is ParkMobile.

Not read: easyparkgroup.com itself (redirect ends in a 404), easypark.com/en and /en-gb (both 404), and the English "About EasyPark" page beyond a skim.

brands.name: Flowbird
brands.description:
Flowbird makes parking and public-transport payment hardware and software. flowbird.group now forwards to www.flowbird.com. Its home page carries the banner "EasyPark Group and Flowbird are now Arrive", which links to arrive.com.

Parking: the on-street page lists pay-and-display terminals and kiosks, including the Strada EVOL GEN 3, Strada TPAL GEN 3, Strada S5 GEN 3, StreetSmart S5 GEN 3, Compact S5 and Access S5. Across the range they take coins, cards, banknotes or city cards depending on the model (the Access S5 is cashless), on solar or mains power. The menu also lists off-street, EV charging, mobile and "Parking business services". Transport: the menu lists Equipment, Open Payment, MaaS and a "Transport Fare Collection Platform". The transport page says Flowbird aims to "optimize investment value for transport authorities and operators". It also lists account-based ticketing, Open Payment and back-office systems. Energy services are sold as Park&Gaz.

The about page claims "6000 Cities" and "Over 80 Countries", and says "84% of the 50 biggest cities in the world rely on Flowbird". Its history starts in 1968 with "The first parking meter is installed on the Paris streets". In 2003 Parkeon was created from Schlumberger's parking and ticketing division. In 2018 "Parkeon and Cale merge to become Flowbird". Since 2020 it has bought Yellowbrick (NL), YourParkingSpace (UK) and Piconet (RO).

US public buyers in its news list include "SEPTA Partners with Flowbird to Launch Advanced Commuter Parking System" (Sept 2024) and "Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) Partners with Flowbird to Modernize Transit System" (Sept 2024). Others are Pittsburgh Regional Transit (Aug 2024), "Flowbird Pay-by-Plate Pay Stations Launch in the City of New York" (June 2024), and Beverly Hills, Charleston SC, Clearwater FL, Rochester and Leavenworth.

Place in Arrive: Flowbird Group announced on November 9, 2023 its decision to be acquired by EasyPark Group, and EasyPark Group closed the purchase on January 15, 2025. Flowbird CEO Frédéric Beylier then left, and Cameron Clayton became CEO of the joint company. Arrive's about page describes Flowbird as delivering "mobility solutions in over 6,000 cities across 80 countries". Arrive's public-transport page sells open payment, validators and bus consoles but does not name Flowbird on that page.

Not read: the Equipment, Open Payment, MaaS and Fare Collection sub-pages. Also unread are Flowbird's own releases on the Yellowbrick, YourParkingSpace and Piconet purchases. The flowbird.com footer still reads "© Flowbird Group 2024", and the newest news item seen is dated May 19, 2025.

brands.name: ParkMobile
brands.description:
ParkMobile, LLC runs a US parking app and the parking-management tools behind it. Its about page says "in 2008, ParkMobile launched" and that drivers can "pay for street and garage parking without having to use a meter or kiosk". It also sells reservations for events, airports and campuses. The footer reads "© 2026 ParkMobile, LLC", and some of its releases carry Atlanta, GA datelines.

Public buyers: the provider menu has "ParkMobile for" pages for Municipalities, Event venues, Private operators, College campuses, and Transit and airports. The municipalities page says "Serving over 600 municipalities". It promises congestion control, flexible payment, links to existing parking hardware and software, analytics and more revenue, and offers a Dashboard product. The transit and airports page sells reservations and multi-location management to "transit operators". City customers named in its own news include:
- the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency (Nov 5, 2025), for "the city's 26,000 on-street parking spaces"
- Buffalo, NY (July 2025), including ParkMobile Insights analytics for the city
- the City of Tacoma (Aug 2026)
- Royal Oak, MI (Jan 2026)
- the Miami Parking Authority
- Durham, NC

Place in Arrive: its 2021 release says it "has been part of BMW and Daimler's mobility joint venture PARK NOW Group since March 2019". On June 1, 2021, EasyPark Group "announced today the completed acquisition of PARK NOW Group, including North American-based ParkMobile". At that point ParkMobile had "25 million users and a presence in over 450 cities". Its current releases call it part of Arrive. The Tacoma release opens "Part of the larger leading global mobility platform Arrive, ParkMobile offers drivers..." and the SFMTA release calls it "part of the global mobility company Arrive". Arrive staff speak for it: Scott Booker, "General Manager of Parking at Arrive", and Benoit Reliquet, Arrive's Head of Parking for North America. Its Careers link goes to careers.arrive.com, and its press contact is [address removed]. Arrive's about page lists it as "the leading provider of smart parking and mobility solutions in North America", "available in over 700 cities".

Not read: the later pages of the newsroom (only page 1 of 30 was listed) and the provider solution pages (Payments, Management, Insights).

profile.description:
Arrive is the Stockholm-based parent company of a group of parking, payment and public-transport brands. Its site footer gives the address "Birger Jarlsgatan 57B, 113 56 Stockholm". Its own release of June 12, 2025 says the name Arrive "will replace EasyPark Group and Flowbird Group" and that it "will be the overarching parent company" for EasyPark, Flowbird, ParkMobile, Parkopedia, RingGo, Yellowbrick, Your Parking Space and other brands. The same release says the consumer brands and apps "will remain unaffected for the foreseeable future". The release boilerplate describes the company as "Present in over 90 countries and 20,000 cities".

The home page sorts the offer into five groups: parking ("digital payments for parking and EV charging"), city planning (mobility data), public transport ("our open payment solution and smart ticketing devices"), fleets and businesses, and in-car services for automakers. Public buyers appear on the solution pages. The public-transport page says "We help operators and local governments simplify ticketing" and lists Open Payment, railway-certified ticket validators, bus driver consoles and vending machines. The city-planner page offers dashboards "for decision-makers" with "policy-grade insights". The parking-operators page lists payment stations, mobile paid parking and in-car payment. Case studies on the home page cover Las Vegas pay stations, a parking app in downtown Detroit, Monaco's MaaS app and Lerici, Italy.

The about page lists the family: EasyPark, Flowbird, RingGo, ParkMobile, Yellowbrick, Parkopedia, YourParkingSpace and Parkimeter. It also has a timeline that starts with Cale's first parking meters in Sweden in 1955 and ends with "2025 Arrive is launched". The leadership page names Cameron Clayton as chief executive and Niklas Savander as board chair. It also says "Arrive is backed by three investment firms: Verdane, Vitruvian Partners, and Searchlight Capital."

The footer Careers link goes to careers.arrive.com and the header Career link to jobs.ashbyhq.com/arrive. Press goes to [address removed], with a named contact for North America.

Not read: the newsroom index printed no article list as text, so only releases found by search were read. The Arrive Magazine PDF was not read. arrive.com/about returns 404; the real about page is /en/about/about-us. The headline counters on the home and about pages printed as "0", so no figures were taken from them.
