profile.description:
Arrive is the Stockholm-based parent company of a group of parking, payment and public-transport brands. Its site footer gives the address "Birger Jarlsgatan 57B, 113 56 Stockholm". Its own release of June 12, 2025 says the name Arrive "will replace EasyPark Group and Flowbird Group" and that it "will be the overarching parent company" for EasyPark, Flowbird, ParkMobile, Parkopedia, RingGo, Yellowbrick, Your Parking Space and other brands. The same release says the consumer brands and apps "will remain unaffected for the foreseeable future". The release boilerplate describes the company as "Present in over 90 countries and 20,000 cities".

The home page sorts the offer into five groups: parking ("digital payments for parking and EV charging"), city planning (mobility data), public transport ("our open payment solution and smart ticketing devices"), fleets and businesses, and in-car services for automakers. Public buyers appear on the solution pages. The public-transport page says "We help operators and local governments simplify ticketing" and lists Open Payment, railway-certified ticket validators, bus driver consoles and vending machines. The city-planner page offers dashboards "for decision-makers" with "policy-grade insights". The parking-operators page lists payment stations, mobile paid parking and in-car payment. Case studies on the home page cover Las Vegas pay stations, a parking app in downtown Detroit, Monaco's MaaS app and Lerici, Italy.

The about page lists the family: EasyPark, Flowbird, RingGo, ParkMobile, Yellowbrick, Parkopedia, YourParkingSpace and Parkimeter. It also has a timeline that starts with Cale's first parking meters in Sweden in 1955 and ends with "2025 Arrive is launched". The leadership page names Cameron Clayton as chief executive and Niklas Savander as board chair. It also says "Arrive is backed by three investment firms: Verdane, Vitruvian Partners, and Searchlight Capital."

The footer Careers link goes to careers.arrive.com and the header Career link to jobs.ashbyhq.com/arrive. Press goes to [address removed], with a named contact for North America.

Not read: the newsroom index printed no article list as text, so only releases found by search were read. The Arrive Magazine PDF was not read. arrive.com/about returns 404; the real about page is /en/about/about-us. The headline counters on the home and about pages printed as "0", so no figures were taken from them.

brands.name: EasyPark (formerly EasyPark Group)
brands.description:
EasyPark Group is the old corporate name of the company now called Arrive. Arrive's June 12, 2025 release says EasyPark Group "unveiled a new name and identity" and that Arrive "will replace EasyPark Group and Flowbird Group". The old corporate site no longer works on its own. easyparkgroup.com forwards to www.easypark.com/en, which returned HTTP 404 when read. easyparkgroup.com/news/ forwards to the Arrive newsroom. One leftover is still live: careers.easyparkgroup.com loads under the title "Together, we make cities more livable! - EasyPark Group".

History from Arrive's about-page timeline: EasyPark was founded in Norway and Denmark in 2000-2001. "Mint acquires Payway and merges with EasyPark" in 2004-2005. EasyPark bought Telepark in Italy in 2014. In 2021 it acquired "Park Now Group, including RingGo and ParkMobile brands, and Parkimeter". It bought MPLA (Czech Republic) and Handyparken (Austria) in 2024, then Flowbird and Parkopedia in 2025. Flowbird's November 2023 release says EasyPark Group "owns and develops the apps EasyPark, ParkMobile, RingGo and Park-line" and operates "in over 4,000 cities across more than 20 countries".

The EasyPark brand still runs its own site at easypark.com. From here it served a Dutch page (/nl) and an English page for Sweden (/en-se). It sells a consumer parking app ("the No.1 parking app in Europe") with pay-by-minute parking, EV charging and in-car parking. For public buyers, its "Cities and operators" page describes "a digital ecosystem where municipal authorities, private garage operators, and drivers, play a part in optimizing the available parking inventory". The services it lists are EasyPark Insights, The Parking Dashboard, EasyPark SmartHUB, Express pay, Digital Permits and EV charging. The page claims "4,400 +" cities and "7,700 +" parking operators. The site footer links "About Arrive" to arrive.com. Arrive's about page calls EasyPark "the leading provider of smart parking and mobility solutions in Europe".

For the board: the corporate body is now Arrive, and EasyPark is its European parking-app brand. No US public buyers appeared on the EasyPark pages read. Arrive's North American app is ParkMobile.

Not read: easyparkgroup.com itself (redirect ends in a 404), easypark.com/en and /en-gb (both 404), and the English "About EasyPark" page beyond a skim.

brands.name: Flowbird
brands.description:
Flowbird makes parking and public-transport payment hardware and software. flowbird.group now forwards to www.flowbird.com. Its home page carries the banner "EasyPark Group and Flowbird are now Arrive", which links to arrive.com.

Parking: the on-street page lists pay-and-display terminals and kiosks, including the Strada EVOL GEN 3, Strada TPAL GEN 3, Strada S5 GEN 3, StreetSmart S5 GEN 3, Compact S5 and Access S5. Across the range they take coins, cards, banknotes or city cards depending on the model (the Access S5 is cashless), on solar or mains power. The menu also lists off-street, EV charging, mobile and "Parking business services". Transport: the menu lists Equipment, Open Payment, MaaS and a "Transport Fare Collection Platform". The transport page says Flowbird aims to "optimize investment value for transport authorities and operators". It also lists account-based ticketing, Open Payment and back-office systems. Energy services are sold as Park&Gaz.

The about page claims "6000 Cities" and "Over 80 Countries", and says "84% of the 50 biggest cities in the world rely on Flowbird". Its history starts in 1968 with "The first parking meter is installed on the Paris streets". In 2003 Parkeon was created from Schlumberger's parking and ticketing division. In 2018 "Parkeon and Cale merge to become Flowbird". Since 2020 it has bought Yellowbrick (NL), YourParkingSpace (UK) and Piconet (RO).

US public buyers in its news list include "SEPTA Partners with Flowbird to Launch Advanced Commuter Parking System" (Sept 2024) and "Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) Partners with Flowbird to Modernize Transit System" (Sept 2024). Others are Pittsburgh Regional Transit (Aug 2024), "Flowbird Pay-by-Plate Pay Stations Launch in the City of New York" (June 2024), and Beverly Hills, Charleston SC, Clearwater FL, Rochester and Leavenworth.

Place in Arrive: Flowbird Group announced on November 9, 2023 its decision to be acquired by EasyPark Group, and EasyPark Group closed the purchase on January 15, 2025. Flowbird CEO Frédéric Beylier then left, and Cameron Clayton became CEO of the joint company. Arrive's about page describes Flowbird as delivering "mobility solutions in over 6,000 cities across 80 countries". Arrive's public-transport page sells open payment, validators and bus consoles but does not name Flowbird on that page.

Not read: the Equipment, Open Payment, MaaS and Fare Collection sub-pages. Also unread are Flowbird's own releases on the Yellowbrick, YourParkingSpace and Piconet purchases. The flowbird.com footer still reads "© Flowbird Group 2024", and the newest news item seen is dated May 19, 2025.

brands.name: EasyPark (formerly EasyPark Group)
brands.description:
EasyPark Group is the old corporate name of the company now called Arrive. Arrive's June 12, 2025 release says EasyPark Group "unveiled a new name and identity" and that Arrive "will replace EasyPark Group and Flowbird Group". The old corporate site no longer works on its own. easyparkgroup.com forwards to www.easypark.com/en, which returned HTTP 404 when read. easyparkgroup.com/news/ forwards to the Arrive newsroom. One leftover is still live: careers.easyparkgroup.com loads under the title "Together, we make cities more livable! - EasyPark Group".

History from Arrive's about-page timeline: EasyPark was founded in Norway and Denmark in 2000-2001. "Mint acquires Payway and merges with EasyPark" in 2004-2005. EasyPark bought Telepark in Italy in 2014. In 2021 it acquired "Park Now Group, including RingGo and ParkMobile brands, and Parkimeter". It bought MPLA (Czech Republic) and Handyparken (Austria) in 2024, then Flowbird and Parkopedia in 2025. Flowbird's November 2023 release says EasyPark Group "owns and develops the apps EasyPark, ParkMobile, RingGo and Park-line" and operates "in over 4,000 cities across more than 20 countries".

The EasyPark brand still runs its own site at easypark.com. From here it served a Dutch page (/nl) and an English page for Sweden (/en-se). It sells a consumer parking app ("the No.1 parking app in Europe") with pay-by-minute parking, EV charging and in-car parking. For public buyers, its "Cities and operators" page describes "a digital ecosystem where municipal authorities, private garage operators, and drivers, play a part in optimizing the available parking inventory". The services it lists are EasyPark Insights, The Parking Dashboard, EasyPark SmartHUB, Express pay, Digital Permits and EV charging. The page claims "4,400 +" cities and "7,700 +" parking operators. The site footer links "About Arrive" to arrive.com. Arrive's about page calls EasyPark "the leading provider of smart parking and mobility solutions in Europe".

For the board: the corporate body is now Arrive, and EasyPark is its European parking-app brand. No US public buyers appeared on the EasyPark pages read. Arrive's North American app is ParkMobile.

Not read: easyparkgroup.com itself (redirect ends in a 404), easypark.com/en and /en-gb (both 404), and the English "About EasyPark" page beyond a skim.

brands.name: Flowbird
brands.description:
Flowbird makes parking and public-transport payment hardware and software. flowbird.group now forwards to www.flowbird.com. Its home page carries the banner "EasyPark Group and Flowbird are now Arrive", which links to arrive.com.

Parking: the on-street page lists pay-and-display terminals and kiosks, including the Strada EVOL GEN 3, Strada TPAL GEN 3, Strada S5 GEN 3, StreetSmart S5 GEN 3, Compact S5 and Access S5. Across the range they take coins, cards, banknotes or city cards depending on the model (the Access S5 is cashless), on solar or mains power. The menu also lists off-street, EV charging, mobile and "Parking business services". Transport: the menu lists Equipment, Open Payment, MaaS and a "Transport Fare Collection Platform". The transport page says Flowbird aims to "optimize investment value for transport authorities and operators". It also lists account-based ticketing, Open Payment and back-office systems. Energy services are sold as Park&Gaz.

The about page claims "6000 Cities" and "Over 80 Countries", and says "84% of the 50 biggest cities in the world rely on Flowbird". Its history starts in 1968 with "The first parking meter is installed on the Paris streets". In 2003 Parkeon was created from Schlumberger's parking and ticketing division. In 2018 "Parkeon and Cale merge to become Flowbird". Since 2020 it has bought Yellowbrick (NL), YourParkingSpace (UK) and Piconet (RO).

US public buyers in its news list include "SEPTA Partners with Flowbird to Launch Advanced Commuter Parking System" (Sept 2024) and "Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) Partners with Flowbird to Modernize Transit System" (Sept 2024). Others are Pittsburgh Regional Transit (Aug 2024), "Flowbird Pay-by-Plate Pay Stations Launch in the City of New York" (June 2024), and Beverly Hills, Charleston SC, Clearwater FL, Rochester and Leavenworth.

Place in Arrive: Flowbird Group announced on November 9, 2023 its decision to be acquired by EasyPark Group, and EasyPark Group closed the purchase on January 15, 2025. Flowbird CEO Frédéric Beylier then left, and Cameron Clayton became CEO of the joint company. Arrive's about page describes Flowbird as delivering "mobility solutions in over 6,000 cities across 80 countries". Arrive's public-transport page sells open payment, validators and bus consoles but does not name Flowbird on that page.

Not read: the Equipment, Open Payment, MaaS and Fare Collection sub-pages. Also unread are Flowbird's own releases on the Yellowbrick, YourParkingSpace and Piconet purchases. The flowbird.com footer still reads "© Flowbird Group 2024", and the newest news item seen is dated May 19, 2025.

paragraphs: Arrive sells urban mobility technology to city governments, parking operators and businesses. On the parking side that means demand insight and digital payments for parking and EV charging.

Drivers start, stop, extend and pay for a session from an app. Operators run payment stations and in-car integrations from the same platform. License plate recognition can start and end sessions automatically as cars enter and leave. The company says its EV solutions connect with more than 400 charge point operators. For city planners, dashboards report parking use, traffic trends and mobility patterns to guide planning.

Arrive describes itself as a coming together of Flowbird Group, EasyPark Group, Parkopedia and others. The about page dates the story back to 1955. That timeline opens with Cale installing its first parking meters. Within the group, Flowbird is described as delivering mobility solutions in over 6,000 cities across 80 countries. EasyPark is described as present in over 4,000 cities across more than 20 countries.

before.description: Digital courtroom recording and speech recognition systems for courts

after.name: CourtSmart
after.description: Digital courtroom recording and speech recognition systems for courts

paragraphs: CourtSmart designs and installs digital audio and video recording systems for courtrooms. The same recording technology is offered for hearing rooms, interview rooms and conferences.

Audio moves from the courtroom to recording servers or workstations over Dante digital transport. A room can record on its own PC or laptop or onto networked central servers, with automatic archiving either way. Staff can annotate proceedings, and the recording system can be tied into a case management system. A docket display application pulls calendar and public access information from the court's case management system.

The company says its recording systems capture millions of hours of legal proceedings in the United States and internationally. Integration is built on ODBC open standards. For remote hearings, a portable system can be taken along and the recordings uploaded afterwards to a central site for permanent storage.

paragraphs: Illuminex AI applies artificial intelligence to inspection work on airfields. The company says it works with industry, government and academia on human-in-the-loop automation meant to increase safety and efficiency in critical infrastructure operations and maintenance.

One capability identifies and logs foreign object debris across runways, taxiways and aprons. Another detects fence damage, breaches and signage integrity issues. Operators are given real-time situational awareness and offset guidance to help them hold required clearances. Winter work is covered by measuring and mapping snowbank profiles. A product listed as coming soon maps runway surface conditions to support maintenance planning.

The team is described as a blend of engineers, technologists, entrepreneurs and industry specialists. Executive experience is listed in finance, non-destructive testing and inspection, AI, and advanced physical process modeling. A testimonial on the home page speaks to investing in technology to improve operational efficiency at Toronto Pearson. A 60 day pilot sign-up is offered on the same page.

paragraphs: FlightBI sells aviation business intelligence to airports, helping their managers read flight distribution, demand growth, traffic origins and destinations, and traveler behavior. It sells to airlines as well, covering market size, demand growth, fare trends and the competitive landscape. Travel management companies are a third audience, using the analysis to read traveler preferences and behavior.

The products are sold as a suite for aviation decision making. One platform analyzes passenger origins at ZIP-code level and measures traffic leakage to competing airports. A separate catchment platform works at the census subdivision level for Canadian airports. A planning platform helps air service development teams find market opportunities and build airline proposals. A forecasting product predicts hourly passenger volumes up to seven days ahead for United States airports.

The company also offers a tool that answers aviation questions posed in ordinary language rather than through a data analyst. Customer comments on the site are attributed to air service development roles at airports that are described but not named.

after.name: Actuate AI
after.description: AI weapon and intruder detection layered on school security cameras

paragraphs: Actuate sells video analytics that detect guns, intruders and crowds in real time and cut down false alarms. The named buyers are security providers, among them central monitoring stations and alarm receiving centers.

The company says its analytics push video through multiple models to hold down false positive alarms. It runs from a cloud platform meant to work with systems already in place, which the company says avoids on-site hardware upgrades. A camera health service checks cameras continuously and flags blurriness, tilting, obstructions or a camera that has gone offline. Alerts cover threats such as unauthorized access and fire detection.
Reporting is offered as a way to see trends and system performance and to plan from them. Line crossing detection is another of the analytics the site lists.

paragraphs: EnvisionWare builds self-service systems that public libraries put in front of their patrons. The company frames the goal as enriching what a library offers the public inside the building and beyond it.

On the patron side, that covers scanning, copying and faxing at the point of service. Payment handling, ecommerce services and other self-service options fill out the rest of the line. Users sit across development services departments including planning, building and engineering. The company says it can be deployed in any city or county regardless of size. It integrates with most major permitting systems and mark-up tools. Blitz says it was founded to transform local government operations through AI. paragraphs: CLEAR sells an annual membership that verifies a traveler's identity and moves them through dedicated airport security lanes. The company describes itself more broadly as an identity business rather than an airport one.

Members can add up to three other people to an account, and CLEAR also handles enrollment and renewal for TSA PreCheck. An app is meant to cover the rest of the travel day, telling a member when to leave home to reach the gate on time. paragraphs: Hera Property Registry runs a registration platform that municipalities and government agencies use to deal with vacant and foreclosed properties. The company presents it as a no-cost solution for local governments managing those properties.

The described sequence starts by identifying at-risk vacant properties. Responsible parties are then contacted and asked to register the property. Enforcement follows, aimed at increasing compliance with the ordinance. The company says it uses artificial intelligence to identify at-risk and foreclosed properties. It credits data analysis and banking connections with working out who is responsible for a property. Registration fees fall on property owners, and Hera collects them and shares them with the municipality. Alongside registration, the company lists compliance monitoring and data management.

A community adopts what Hera calls a best-practice ordinance to put the service in place. The fee revenue is framed as generating funds for affordable housing and other community-benefiting initiatives. Testimonials on the site are attributed to local officials, including a city administrator who says the system is making a measurable difference in Moline.

paragraphs: Connectpoint makes digital signage for transit, placed indoors and outdoors at bus stops, shelters, stations, and transit hubs. Its core product is a solar and battery-powered ePaper display showing real-time passenger information. The company describes itself as a provider of solar-powered ePaper signage across the U.S.

The signs connect over 4G or an existing WiFi network and run around the clock on solar or battery power. They show real-time data such as GTFS real-time or any API feed format, or scheduled times instead. Several sizes and styles are offered. No electrical infrastructure is required at the stop. For stations and transit centers there is SmartStop, a kiosk whose 55 inch touch screen carries easy-to-read information and customized route planning. It includes citywide turn-by-turn directions for driving, biking, and walking. An LED line is customized in size and shape for each deployment.

All of it is run from the Connectpoint Asset Management system, which manages and monitors the signage remotely. An agency can start with one sign and expand the network later. The ePaper sign, called the Falcon, is solar-powered, ADA compliant, and carries a five-year warranty. Location-based advertising on the kiosks is offered as a way for an agency to generate revenue.

paragraphs: Bidgely builds energy analytics software for electric utilities, working from the data their smart meters already collect. The core claim is that a utility can identify what is running inside every home and business from meter data alone, with no surveys or smart plugs.

The platform, called UtilityAI, breaks that meter signal down to appliance level for every customer, grid asset and hour of the year. Utilities use it on the customer side to resolve high bill questions before people call in. On the grid side it is pitched for capacity planning that accounts for distributed energy resources. Program teams are offered targeting for EV and electrification enrollment. There is also a module for discovering and remedying energy theft. The company offers the software as SaaS or deployed inside a utility's own cloud.

Buyers span the utility enterprise, covering customer experience, grid operations and efficiency and electrification programs. Case studies on the site report results such as 238% of contracted savings in the first year of a deployment. Bidgely also runs an annual conference, registration for which is advertised on the home page.

paragraphs: Ivalua sells a procurement platform built for supplier and spend management. It is meant to cover indirect goods, services, direct materials and complex categories in one place.

The source-to-pay product unifies intake, source-to-contract, supplier management and procure-to-pay on one data model. Intake management gives employees a central hub for requests, which are routed automatically to the right workflow, owner and system. Source-to-contract carries a purchase from intake and supplier evaluation through contract execution and spend visibility in one connected system. At the far end, accounts payable automation covers invoice capture, global compliance and supplier visibility. The platform offers low-code and no-code configuration and integrates with existing ERP systems.

The company says hundreds of well-known brands use the platform. It also claims a customer retention record spanning more than twenty years. Ivalua cites its placement as a Leader in a 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant report on source-to-pay suites.

paragraphs: CobbleStone Software sells Contract Insight, contract lifecycle management software with agentic features, flexible processes, and AI. Enterprise Edition is built for large organizations seeking full-spectrum contract lifecycle control. Express Edition is a modular, entry-level platform for growing organizations. WorkGroup Edition is deployed locally for midsize teams that want more data control and security.

Contracts sit in a central repository designed for speed and simplicity. Users can add fields, configure workflows without coding, and adapt modules as the business changes. Version history, redlines, and amendments are tracked throughout the lifecycle. An AI layer called VISDOM parses static documents into structured, queryable entities. An organization defines its playbook once, and VISDOM enforces it across drafts, versions, and revisions, flagging deviations before signature. The system unifies data across ERP, CRM, and HR systems.

The company says client documents are processed rather than used to train models. It says clause libraries are configured in hours from existing CLM metadata. Enterprise-wide deployment is usually completed within 60 days, according to the site. The site claims over 30 years of contract lifecycle management work. It addresses legal and procurement teams. On the access side, the company describes an evolution from XGS-PON toward 50G PON and beyond. Its Xtreme Access software manages the access service chain from customer premise equipment through optical network elements to the edge of the internet. That software is meant to run third-party gear as well, including gateways, OLTs, switches and BNGs. A separate fiber extension line uses Gfast over copper already in place to deliver fiber-like speeds where the last hop is hard to build. Those distribution point units can be reverse powered from a network termination device inside the home.

Buyers are addressed as operators capitalizing on government and private investor funded multi-gigabit broadband rollouts. Company news on the home page includes the opening of a research and development center in Hanoi, Vietnam. Its blog index writes about middle-mile networks for utilities and electric cooperatives.

paragraphs: Wavetronix makes radar sensors that detect the presence of vehicles at the stop bar. The buyers are traffic agencies, and the collected data can be shared among several of them. That data feeds uses such as trip times and congestion alerts.

One system is a multi-approach stop bar detector designed for smaller intersections. It covers four approaches of three lanes or less per approach. The flagship stop bar detector sees both moving and stopped vehicles. A safety product tracks vehicles in the dilemma zone out to 600 feet. An extended range version protects large trucks and buses out to 900 feet. A cabinet device supplies power and communication for two to six sensors. A newer add-on analyzes split failures and turning movement counts and recommends updated max green times.

The company says it opened in 2000. All sensors are made at its headquarters in Springville, Utah. It states that it supports and complies with the Build America Buy America Act. It also says it is driven to succeed for customers, not for investors or shareholders.

paragraphs: EYERIDE sells a fleet management system that pulls vehicle and driver data into one place for the organizations that run vehicles. The company pitches the result as an IoT solution for any industry.

Cameras anchor the system, with live views and the ability to go back months to retrieve recorded footage. Driver assistance features track following distance, lane departure and the distance to other vehicles, pedestrians or objects. A driver-facing camera reads behavior in the cab, including fatigue, smoking, phone use and an unfastened seatbelt. Warnings for harsh braking, harsh cornering, speeding and traffic violations reach both the cab and the office. Geofencing lets a manager draw areas and get alerts whenever a vehicle enters or leaves one.

For hours-of-service compliance there is a logging app kept to a handful of sections. In-vehicle cellular routers add connectivity, and the 5G model is offered with SASE options including zero trust security. Operators carrying passengers can add a counter that records how many people enter and exit at any given moment. One described use is school transport, where the tools can let educators and parents know the vehicle location. The site claims thousands of users of the platform for fleet operations.

paragraphs: 911 Tech sells one software system that an agency uses in place of multiple apps, spreadsheets and paper forms. The company says the software was designed by cops for cops, with the aim of making the job easier.

A quartermaster module issues equipment, requires signatures and tracks inventory quantities, with self-service request and acknowledgment workflows for employees. The software is hosted on Amazon Web Services CJIS compliant Gov Cloud. 911 Tech is an official 2026 FBINAA Strategic Alliance Partner. A prior agency training supervisor developed the training tracking module. Support runs around the clock through an online user manual, training and a support desk.

paragraphs: Frost Solutions sells road weather monitoring hardware and software for the crews who fight snow and ice. The stated audience is municipalities and contractors.

The core device is a solar-powered unit that mounts easily and captures hyperlocal weather data every minute. It tracks road surface temperature, grip and coefficient of friction forecasts, air conditions and visibility. Site-level readings also cover pavement temperature, humidity, dew point and frost. The software reviews site photos and weather data every minute and raises an alert when conditions change. Its dashboard carries snow and frost alerts, surface temperature updates and hyperlocal 72-hour forecasts.

Contractors are told to put units in customer parking lots to decide where to send crews first. School districts are another named market, where campuses and multiple buildings are hard to cover. The site says it serves communities in 37 states and 7 provinces.

One pilot can control multiple suppression craft. Those craft carry hundreds of pounds of Class A foam and use autonomous targeting with infrared and video to verify and knock down hot spots. A full system of four to six drones is said to deliver 500 to 1000 pounds of suppression per trip, refillable without fixed infrastructure. Launch is meant to happen from a mobile tablet the moment a fire is spotted, even without a precise location. The copters are built to be carried, with no helipads, mechanics or refueling stations required.

Listed uses run from early response and structure protection to spot fires, mop up, hazmat, utility safety and night operations. The company also says the systems improve the safety and efficiency of prescribed burns. A headline on the site announces that Aspen Fire acquired a Seneca strike team. The founding team is described as fire professionals who teach and fight wildland fire, together with technology entrepreneurs.

paragraphs: GET Group North America sells identity systems for capturing, adjudicating and managing identities, ending in the issuance of secure credentials. The credentials it names run from driver's licenses and ID cards to mobile IDs, passports, and corporate and governmental IDs.

Its CoreID platform pairs biometric capture and facial recognition with back-end database functions, issuing and tracking physical or digital credentials through their lifecycle. It can run in the cloud or on a customer's own premises. Hardware sold alongside the software includes printers for identification cards, security credentials, and access management. A compact enrollment camera is built for high-volume settings and captures ICAO compliant images.

The camera software adjusts automatically for variations in a person's height and distance from the lens. The company says its mobile ID and verification apps for iOS and Android pass a UL conformity assessment against ISO 18013-5 interoperability standards. A news headline on the home page states that the mobile ID is accepted at TSA PreCheck. The digital product is described as putting a high assurance identity on a user's own device.

paragraphs: Schoolyear sells exam security software that turns a student's own laptop into a controlled workspace for a digital exam. The workspace lets desktop applications run in an isolated environment on the student device, with nothing to install.

During an exam the workspace takes over the full screen, closes other applications, and limits students to content the institution approved. Staff decide what is allowed, whitelisting websites, files, or desktop applications by hand. A detection layer sits on top, alerting the proctor when the lock is broken or when virtual machines, remote access, or screen capture appear. The company says this happens without screen recording or monitoring.

The pitch is aimed at institutions that want to scale exams on student owned devices instead of buying more lab seats. Institutions quoted on the site include Wageningen University & Research, which says it wanted flexible fraud prevention for exams on students' own laptops. Another page says TU Delft implemented the software in two weeks and ran an exam for 800 students.

paragraphs: Imagry sells autonomous driving software for public transportation, aimed at the operators who run buses and fleets. It draws a line between itself and robotaxi companies, pointing instead at the commercial transit market.

The approach does without high-definition maps and without LiDAR. Cameras placed around the vehicle gather what the system needs in real time. Neural networks trained by imitating skilled human driving handle the decisions. Nothing depends on the cloud, since everything needed to drive autonomously sits inside the vehicle.

The company says it is running a public bus pilot on an 8 km route in the city of Nahariya, and that it has deployed an autonomous shuttle at a large medical facility. It claims the first autonomous bus to achieve an NCAP safety rating and to comply with the UN-R155 cybersecurity regulation. It also describes partnerships with several international vehicle makers to supply autonomous-driving ready vehicles.

paragraphs: Colaj sells a classroom tool it describes as collaborative AI to bring active learning to every classroom. It is aimed at instructors and their students, with a one-time classroom setup that works every session.

During a lecture it produces live captions and key topics, surfaced by AI as the instructor teaches. It listens to the lecture and drafts poll questions from what the instructor just said. Students answer in their own words, and those answers are clustered into comprehension bands that surface the misconception hiding inside them. After class the tool automatically generates a study guide from each session. The instructor dashboard turns each class into a trend line.

The company grounds the design in education research, citing a review of 225 studies that compared traditional lectures with active-learning sections. Colaj says it is piloting now with instructors and universities. It was launched by an MIT-founded design studio with 20 years of experience.

A scope review step checks draft scopes for gaps, risks and potential barriers to entry for small business before they go public. A solicitation builder drafts documents from an agency's own templates, from RFx packages to purchase orders and contracts. One case study describes a large state producing first drafts in under 15 minutes instead of more than 40 hours. The site states SOC 2 Type II certification. It also says agency data stays with the agency and is not shared even between departments.

paragraphs: Inclusion Solutions sells universally designed access products to businesses and government agencies. The catalog runs to accessible voting booths, polling place supplies and election signage.

Its Franklin voting booth meets ADA and ADAAG standards for width, approach and clearance, and includes one lowered station. Its push button is described as ADA compliant and needing minimal pressure to operate. A flashing strobe provides a silent alert for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. The company also sells Pocketalk, a handheld translator it positions against Section 203 requirements. The alert system is pitched for town halls, schools, public facilities and private businesses. The company says over 35,000 of the booths are in use in 48 states. It says Pocketalk is in use at hundreds of government offices nationwide and at election offices in multiple states. Real-time language interpretation and ADA surveying and analysis are also listed among its offerings.

ClearWorld traces its beginning to a patented idea in Louisiana. Remote area electrification is among the uses the site lists. Controls and real-time monitoring are described as optimizing how the installed systems perform. Literature offered for download includes a document on the RetroFlex systems.

paragraphs: Zensors sells AI meant to automate processes in the physical world, between people, buildings and machines. It describes itself as an AI company building multimodal physical AI that learns to perceive the world with human level accuracy.

The system ingests data from sensors, cameras and other devices and merges it with text and metadata from data warehouses into one aligned format. Models then run across video, time-series and text to build an understanding of a space and the activity inside it. On top of that sit agents intended to automate operational decisions rather than only report them. The company says its models arrive pre-trained on billions of images, videos and text specific to each vertical, so no extensive retraining is required. It also says output is written for IT, operations and business stakeholders while individual customers stay anonymous.

The models are sold as industry-specific and pre-trained for particular kinds of large, complex spaces. Airports are one of the settings its published guidance addresses. The company was spun out of Carnegie Mellon University. Its stated mission is to let anyone create and manage AI without a doctorate in machine learning. Its leadership page describes a head of product and technology steering the system toward suggesting actions that optimize operations.

Submeters on individual tenants let property managers bill back by actual volume rather than by an even split.

The company says its systems are installed at over 1,000 properties in the United States, across multifamily, office, retail, hospitality, and mixed use buildings. paragraphs: In A Blink sells a wireless data link for transit vehicles, described as a drop-in replacement for Wi-Fi that is up to 200 times faster. The point of it is that an operator can offload all the data from a bus or a railcar in minutes instead of hours.

Instead of radio, the patent pending approach uses what the company calls Quantum Communication technology to make Virtual Fibre Optics possible. The optical link works on invisible light. An on-board router adds 4G, LTE and 5G cellular with dual-SIM support for real-time transmissions. The result the company describes is that data is stored at the command center instead of on the vehicles.

The data in question is what transit vehicles collect as they operate, covering telemetry, fare collection, health monitoring, and security. Among the benefits the company claims is quicker resolution of crimes and claims through reliable access to data. It also says the system uses existing infrastructure and operational rules to fit into an agency's IT architecture.

paragraphs: Comsof Fiber is automated planning and design software for telecom operators and engineering firms that need to scale fiber-optic networks quickly and cheaply. The product now belongs to IQGeo, which acquired Comsof NV in August 2022.

The claim made for it is that automation and optimization algorithms cut the end-to-end planning and design process by as much as 90 percent. The same optimization is said to strip out costly design choices and reuse existing infrastructure, lowering total build cost by up to 10 percent. Engineers can compare area costs, scenarios and architectures before settling on a design. Workflow templates let newer engineers repeat an established process and adjust the design outputs.

Two buyers are addressed directly, and network operators are told that legacy planning tools rarely scale to the demands of new deployments. Engineering design firms are told that hand-building multiple design scenarios does not hold up at higher volumes of fiber connections. The page states that IQGeo has over 100,000 active software users among fiber, telecom and utility companies worldwide.

paragraphs: Decision Optimization Technology sells asset management and capital planning software for organizations maintaining aging infrastructure. It provides data management and life-cycle cost optimization across all asset classes.

Instead of prioritization alone, it applies years of doctorate-level research on optimization algorithms to build customized multiyear, multi-constraint capital plans. Users collect and maintain inventory data, condition data, and historical repairs across asset types. Map-centric visualizations display condition and other performance indicators by asset type. Risk-based analysis develops models of asset criticality and likelihood of failure. An unlimited number of scenarios can be set to investigate budgeting strategies, policy decisions, and treatment options. Deterioration models are customizable across asset classes. The product runs as a fully web-based application.

Reports come out presentation ready. The company cites a survey by Infrastructure Solutions Inc. of 100 government clients finding that planning decisions are heavily influenced by socio-economic factors. The site notes that Hanson Professional Services Inc. recommends licensing the software. It also discloses that Hanson owns a significant interest in the licensing entity.

paragraphs: Evidence Grade supplies recordable media for storing evidence, including optical discs, USB cards and solid-state drives. Different grades are matched to different storage conditions. A second grade is intended for semi-controlled conditions that are easier on the disc. The company says it has supplied this media to the law enforcement community since 2009. It also describes itself as the sole source of several branded grades of optical media.

paragraphs: GMV builds software for transit agencies that keeps information clear and connected, from dispatch to drivers to riders. Two dispatch products split that market, with GMV Sync as the fully integrated option for small and mid-sized agencies and ITS Suite adding capabilities and customizations for large ones.

The computer-aided dispatch and automatic vehicle location technology tracks a fleet in real time. Dispatchers can filter and search for vehicles meeting criteria such as being on specific routes or running off schedule. Other tools improve the spacing between vehicles from a single screen. Reports export in PDF, Excel, and CSV format, or arrive as scheduled automated emails. Riders get arrival predictions and service alerts through websites, phone-based interactive voice response systems, SMS text messages, and digital signs. Auto-generated GTFS and GTFS-RT feeds share the same information with applications like Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Transit. A white-labeled app carries real-time arrival predictions and live bus maps under an agency's own branding.

The products are pitched as built for transit agencies of all sizes. The company describes its job as helping agencies provide mobility for transit riders in big cities and small towns across the United States. A headline on the site points to keeping LADOT moving through 2030. Visitors are invited to get to know the US-based team behind the products.

quote.text: We create powerful, intuitive tools for the people who make transit work.

paragraphs: DacraTech sells back-office software for municipal enforcement, covering automated photo enforcement, electronic citations and adjudication. paragraphs: Masabi sells fare payment technology to public transport agencies through a platform called Justride. Its account-based approach lets a passenger travel with a mobile phone, a contactless bank card or a smartcard.

The platform covers smart card, open payment, mobile ticketing, barcode and mobility-as-a-service through a suite of APIs and SDKs. A ready-to-go version arrives pre-integrated with validators, apps, payment gateways and acquiring banks. An open architecture with APIs, SDKs and pre-integrations is meant to make the system easier to implement and operate. The company says the platform is cloud-native and designed to scale for large cities and complex transit systems.

Masabi traces its start to launching the first UK mobile ticketing application with Chiltern Railways in 2007. It says it launched the first mobile ticketing deployment for a United States transit agency in 2012. The about page lists a London office address. It also lists addresses in Denver, Colorado, and in Cluj-Napoca, Romania.

paragraphs: Enevo sells waste container sensors and a cloud software platform to haulers, waste services companies, property managers, cities and campuses that want a clearer picture of their waste operations. The stated point of collecting that data is to let an operator control collection better and improve recycling rates.

Sensors report hourly fill levels and collection events, and the platform turns those readings into trends showing when a container needs picking up. An alert system flags sudden build ups and unforeseen events such as theft, fire or vandalism. A routing engine and scheduler compares service needs against available truck resources and proposes changes based on fill level trends and seasonal variation. Drivers work from an app built around routing, navigation and reporting. Historical fill and collection data can be pulled into other systems through a REST API.

The company says it was founded in 2010 by veterans of the wireless and telecom industry. Its customers run from small regional recyclers to large national waste management companies. Enevo also names property managers, cities, municipalities and higher education and corporate campuses among the groups whose waste data needs it serves.

paragraphs: Hach sells water analysis products to water quality professionals, a group the company numbers at one million. The lineup includes benchtop spectrophotometers, among them a new DR4900 presented as an update to an older design. Process analyzers include a phosphate model presented as a way to stay compliant.

Instruments are paired with reagents made specifically to work with them. Vial tests carry a barcode that lets the spectrophotometer detect the method on its own, averaging ten readings and rejecting outliers. Those vials measure ammonia, nitrate, phosphate, total chlorine, and more with pre-programmed methods. Another format seals all chemicals and processes inside a single self-contained key for portable analyzers. A recurring order program handles reagents, maintenance kits, and supplies needed on a regular basis.

The chemistry pages cite over 75 years of experience. Vial tests and photometers are described as elements of both process control and compliance monitoring. The homepage notes a Silver Medal from EcoVadis for sustainability efforts.

paragraphs: Glacier makes sorting robots for recycling plants, pairing computer vision with mechanical picking to pull more material off the line. The company sells to two audiences at once: the material recovery facilities that run those lines, and consumer brands that want to know what becomes of their packaging.

The robots are compact and built to recover plastics, film and flexibles, paper, OCC, and metals. Behind the picking sit vision models the company says were trained on billions of real recycling images. Operators follow the results on dashboards that report down to the individual item.

Glacier says its robots are built specifically for material recovery facilities, with AI giving visibility at the item level. paragraphs: Eagle Eye Networks sells AI-powered surveillance video for security and business operations. Its main product is the Eagle Eye Cloud Video Management System. The system works with more than 7,500 cameras, so customers do not have to rip out and replace what they already own.

Video can be stored in the cloud, on-premise, or both. AI detects and classifies objects and people. Users search for people, vehicles, and objects by typing what they are looking for. Alerts can give immediate warnings for restricted area breaches. One option connects cameras to the video service without an on-site appliance. That setup suits locations requiring between 1 and 6 cameras per site.

An API platform handles interfacing with cameras, recording video, transmitting and storing it, and making it available to other applications. The company provides integrations with applications such as point-of-sale, access control, and analytics. Video data is stored on its own data centers and encrypted both in transmission and at rest. It cites end-to-end encryption, triple-redundant storage, and SOC 2 compliance. Cameras can also be shared automatically with emergency services.

paragraphs: BusWhere sells real-time bus tracking to schools and districts, so staff can watch buses on a map and spend less time answering phone calls from parents asking where the bus is. Parents get a notification on their phone when the bus is getting close and can watch it move toward the stop. The same tracking is sold for shuttle fleets at corporate headquarters, hospitals, rental car companies, hotels and airports.

Routes are set up in minutes with drag and drop route creation. Setup handles drop-a-pin stops, off-road stops in parking lots, circular routes and multiple buses on one route. Vehicle data covers fuel levels, odometer and sudden braking. The resulting logs are interactive and downloadable. Operators can also bring existing hardware, since the product integrates with Geotab, Samsara, Zonar and others.

Administrators using the product are said to report a drop in calls asking when the bus will arrive, along with higher rider satisfaction. For bus companies, the process is to plug the tracker in on the bus, register online and start tracking. Schools are told they can be running in under an hour. The site lists an address in North Bethesda, Maryland. It also cites a United States patent.

paragraphs: The site at identakid.com presents CENTEGIX Visitu, which helps schools manage campus access through digital visitor check-in, identification, monitoring and reporting. Visitu sits beside other safety products on the site, including a wearable panic button called CrisisAlert. before.name: Evidence Grade
before.why: Only two pages, but the about page states plainly what the media is, who buys it, how it is tested and how long the company has done it.

paragraphs.text: Evidence Grade supplies recordable media for storing evidence, including optical discs, USB cards and solid-state drives.

paragraphs.text: The buyers it names are government agencies, prosecutors, district attorneys, courts, and law enforcement organizations at the state, local and county level.

paragraphs.text: Those buyers, the company says, need media that stays readable until after the last appeal.
paragraphs.quote: These organizations require that any media used for original or derived evidence must be readable until after the last appeal.

paragraphs.text: Different grades are matched to different storage conditions.
paragraphs.quote: The Evidence Grade ® media is for use where recording and storage may be under adverse environmental and physical conditions.

paragraphs.text: A second grade is intended for semi-controlled conditions that are easier on the disc.
paragraphs.quote: Judicial Grade™ media is for use under semi-controlled conditions that are less detrimental to the life of the media.

paragraphs.text: Discs can carry human and machine-readable serialization meant to support chain of evidence procedures.
paragraphs.quote: Human and machine-readable serialization can strengthen the chain of evidence procedures.

paragraphs.text: The company describes inspection at intake and during manufacturing, with anything non-compliant thrown out.
paragraphs.quote: As a result of these procedures, any non-compliant media is scrapped.

paragraphs.text: The company says it has supplied this media to the law enforcement community since 2009.
paragraphs.quote: has been the source for Evidence Grade ® media for the Law Enforcement community since 2009.

paragraphs.text: It states that its testing is meant to keep media readable for at least thirty-two years under adverse and semi-controlled conditions.
paragraphs.quote: will survive the use, handling, and storage under adverse and semi-controlled conditions for at least 32 years

paragraphs.quote: is now the sole source of Evidence Grade ® , Judicial Grade™, Law Enforcement Grade™, and Discovery Grade™ media, including CD-R, DVD-R DVD±R, BD-R, BD-R-DL, and BD-RXL

quote.text: These organizations require that any media used for original or derived evidence must be readable until after the last appeal.

before.name: Imagry
before.why: A single long homepage covers the product, the technical approach, two deployments, and the safety claims, with no deeper pages to confirm them.

paragraphs.text: Imagry sells autonomous driving software for public transportation, aimed at the operators who run buses and fleets.
paragraphs.quote: Safe, certified, and operational autonomous driving solutions for bus and fleet operators.

paragraphs.text: It draws a line between itself and robotaxi companies, pointing instead at the commercial transit market.
paragraphs.quote: Unlike robotaxis, our solutions serve the commercial transit market

paragraphs.text: The approach does without high-definition maps and without LiDAR.
paragraphs.quote: eliminates the need for maps or LiDAR, and runs on the vehicles you already build

paragraphs.text: Cameras placed around the vehicle gather what the system needs in real time.
paragraphs.quote: Multiple 360° strategically-located cameras collect all necessary information in real time.

paragraphs.text: Neural networks trained by imitating skilled human driving handle the decisions.
paragraphs.quote: Our bio-inspired neural network learns how to operate the vehicle by imitating skilled human driving behavior.

paragraphs.text: Nothing depends on the cloud, since everything needed to drive autonomously sits inside the vehicle.
paragraphs.quote: No cloud dependencies or infrastructure modifications required; everything needed to drive autonomously is located within the vehicle.

paragraphs.text: The company says it is running a public bus pilot on an 8 km route in the city of Nahariya, and that it has deployed an autonomous shuttle at a large medical facility.
paragraphs.quote: Imagry is operating a public bus pilot program on an 8 km route in the city of Nahariya.

paragraphs.text: It claims the first autonomous bus to achieve an NCAP safety rating and to comply with the UN-R155 cybersecurity regulation.
paragraphs.quote: The first autonomous bus to achieve an NCAP safety rating and comply with the UN-R155 cybersecurity regulation.

paragraphs.text: It also describes partnerships with several international vehicle makers to supply autonomous-driving ready vehicles.
paragraphs.quote: We have partnered with multiple international OEMs to provide autonomous-driving ready vehicles worldwide.

quote.text: Billions have been spent chasing driverless cars. Most still rely on HD maps, expensive sensors, and rigid logic, and fail in the real world.

before.name: Schoolyear
before.why: Only two pages, both product focused, but they describe the exam workspace, its blocking and detection layers, and name institutions quoted on the site; nothing about founding, size, or funding.

paragraphs.text: Schoolyear sells exam security software that turns a student's own laptop into a controlled workspace for a digital exam.
paragraphs.quote: Transform any device into a secure, controlled exam workspace.

paragraphs.text: The workspace lets desktop applications run in an isolated environment on the student device, with nothing to install.
paragraphs.quote: enabling these applications to run in a fully isolated environment on any student device, without software installation.

paragraphs.text: During an exam the workspace takes over the full screen, closes other applications, and limits students to content the institution approved.
paragraphs.quote: The Safe Exam Workspace locks into full-screen mode, closes other applications and ensures that students have access only to pre-approved content.

paragraphs.text: Staff decide what is allowed, whitelisting websites, files, or desktop applications by hand.
paragraphs.quote: Manually whitelist websites, files, or desktop applications

paragraphs.text: A detection layer sits on top, alerting the proctor when the lock is broken or when virtual machines, remote access, or screen capture appear.
paragraphs.quote: The dashboard will alert the proctor if Schoolyear isn't locked to full-screen or if other software, like virtual machines, remote access, or screen capturing is used.

paragraphs.text: The company says this happens without screen recording or monitoring.
paragraphs.quote: no screen recording or monitoring needed

paragraphs.text: The pitch is aimed at institutions that want to scale exams on student owned devices instead of buying more lab seats.
paragraphs.quote: Utilize Schoolyear on student-owned devices to transform any room into a temporary exam computer lab.

paragraphs.text: Institutions quoted on the site include Wageningen University & Research, which says it wanted flexible fraud prevention for exams on students' own laptops.
paragraphs.quote: Wageningen University & Research sought a flexible solution for fraud prevention during exams administered on students' own laptops.

paragraphs.text: Another page says TU Delft implemented the software in two weeks and ran an exam for 800 students.
paragraphs.quote: Learn how TU delft implemented Schoolyear in 2 weeks and took an exam of 800 students

quote.text: Stop AI cheating in digital exams

paragraphs.text: Citylogix sells municipal asset and work order management software, pitched at communities of every size.
paragraphs.quote: Smarter Asset Management for Communities of All Sizes

paragraphs.text: It also collects the data that feeds the software, driving streets with LiDAR and 360-degree imaging to map road conditions and right-of-way assets.

paragraphs.text: Inside the software, work orders are tied to the assets themselves and travel from the office to the crew and back.
paragraphs.quote: Citylogix links work orders directly to your assets, eliminating inefficiencies. Work orders move seamlessly from the office to the field and back again

paragraphs.text: Machine learning grades pavement distress and turns it into heatmaps of the worst stretches.
paragraphs.quote: Our machine-learning powered pavement distress analysis, surface differentiation, and heatmaps provide precise insights into problem areas

paragraphs.text: Sidewalk and ADA ramp condition assessment is offered alongside the road work.
paragraphs.quote: Sidewalk & ADA Ramp Condition Assessment

paragraphs.text: Budget and capital planning tools are meant to help a public works director justify what gets funded.
paragraphs.quote: Maximize funding, justify investments, and optimize spending

paragraphs.text: Resident service requests drop into the same work order queue.
paragraphs.quote: Service requests flow seamlessly into work orders

paragraphs.text: The customers are municipalities across North America.
paragraphs.quote: Municipalities in North America have chosen Citylogix

paragraphs.text: The company reports miles under management in 40 states, four provinces and one territory.
paragraphs.quote: miles under management in 40 states, 4 provinces & 1 territory

paragraphs.text: It also counts ramps assessed for ADA and AODA compliance among its results.
paragraphs.quote: Ramps assessed for ADA/AODA Compliance

paragraphs.text: A recent announcement describes a partnership with NIRA Dynamics for continuous, IRI-based road monitoring using survey vehicles.
paragraphs.quote: NIRA Dynamics announce a partnership delivering continuous, IRI-based road monitoring via survey vehicles

paragraphs.text: The contact block lists an address on Salem Street in Wakefield, Massachusetts.
paragraphs.quote: 605 Salem Street Wakefield MA 01880

before.name: Aladtec (TCP Software)
before.why: One marketing page under the TCP Software brand, concrete about the scheduling problem it solves but thin on company detail.

paragraphs.text: Aladtec is scheduling software for agencies that have to staff every hour of the day.
paragraphs.quote: Aladtec scheduling software helps fire, EMS, law enforcement, and corrections agencies ensure shift coverage, comply with union and labor rules, and retain employees.

paragraphs.text: It is sold under TimeClock Plus, LLC, which trades as TCP Software.
paragraphs.quote: TimeClock Plus, LLC (TCP Software). All rights reserved.

paragraphs.text: Schedules are built on rotational shift patterns, and open shifts are filled automatically so coverage holds.
paragraphs.quote: Aladtec fills every shift automatically, so your agency stays emergency ready around the clock.

paragraphs.text: Work, union and fatigue rules are written into each schedule, which is the basis of the audit readiness claim.
paragraphs.quote: Aladtec builds your work, union, and fatigue rules right into every schedule

paragraphs.text: Reporting is meant to show where labor dollars go as overtime accumulates.
paragraphs.quote: Aladtec shows you exactly where your labor dollars go so you can protect your budget

paragraphs.text: Staff see their own schedules and handle trades and pickups themselves.
paragraphs.quote: plus self-service trades and pickups

paragraphs.text: One testimonial on the page is credited to Manassas Park Fire and Rescue.
paragraphs.quote: Manassas Park Fire and Rescue

paragraphs.text: A resource listed on the page describes the Minnesota Department of Corrections scheduling across nine facilities.
paragraphs.quote: Minnesota Department of Corrections Simplified Scheduling Across Nine Facilities with Aladtec

paragraphs.text: Government and public safety appears as one of the industries the site asks about.
paragraphs.quote: Government & public safety

quote.text: Public safety scheduling software built for 24/7 agencies

paragraphs.quote: Generate reports for corridors, intersections, before-after studies, or safety KPIs

paragraphs.quote: Optimizes signal timing in real time to reduce delays, improve fuel efficiency

before.name: Daupler
before.description: After-hours call intake, incident triage and crew dispatch software for water, sewer and electric utilities and public works departments - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: Daupler sells a response management system that gives teams the information and tools to respond to service requests and emergencies. Public works, utilities, and service organizations of all sizes are named as the users. The work runs from odor complaints to water main breaks.

The company runs call centers that take intake calls, notify staff about urgent issues, and document noncritical calls for the next day. An automated roster callout feature forms crews without anyone working a phone list by hand. Event detection spots incidents affecting multiple people and stops repeat calls from being dispatched. For outbound messages, the system sends a text or a recorded voice message depending on whether the number is mobile or a landline. The platform sits at the center of existing information systems and combines their data into one view of an incident. Site arrival times and crew check-ins are logged to help make sure crews get back safely.
The company states clients are seeing a 20-75% reduction in callouts. Its pages describe the City of Durham integrating the system with CityWorks.

before.name: Aquasight
before.description: AI operations and forecasting software for water and wastewater utilities - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: Aquasight sells analytics software for the people who run water and wastewater utilities. The company says the software runs in the cloud and calls for no new hardware.

before.name: Hach (Veralto)
before.description: Water quality instrumentation and analytics for municipal water and wastewater plants - exhibited at WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: Hach sells water analysis products to water quality professionals, a group the company numbers at one million. The lineup includes benchtop spectrophotometers, among them a new DR4900 presented as an update to an older design. Process analyzers include a phosphate model presented as a way to stay compliant.

Instruments are paired with reagents made specifically to work with them. Vial tests carry a barcode that lets the spectrophotometer detect the method on its own, averaging ten readings and rejecting outliers. Those vials measure ammonia, nitrate, phosphate, total chlorine, and more with pre-programmed methods. Kando states that the platform uses IoT devices, AI, and LLM to identify upstream wastewater quality discharges and to protect WWTP processes.

A further component named on the homepage is an Assessment map, presented as a way to prioritize daily operations, pre-treatment activities, and strategic objectives. before.name: ADS Environmental Services (IDEX)
before.description: Sewer flow monitoring and I&I analytics for municipal wastewater utilities - exhibited at WEFTEC 2026, StormCon 2026

paragraphs: ADS Environmental Services provides flow, level and rainfall monitoring for wastewater, storm and surface water systems. The buyers are municipal owners who need to know what is happening in their collection systems when it rains. The problems addressed include sanitary sewer overflows, sewer cleaning, combined sewer overflows and inflow and infiltration.

Monitors in the sewer feed software for visualizing, analyzing and managing the network. An agency can buy the equipment and run the program with its own staff. At the other end of the range, the company handles everything from placing the equipment to sending the alerts. A newer offering applies machine learning to spot developing blockages early enough to act on them.

Peter Petroff established the company in 1975 after a NASA career as a lunar guidance system engineer. A network of more than 400 monitors in Sydney, Australia in 1990 is described as a milestone in the company history. Product quality management certifications have been held since 1994, including an ISO 9001:2015 certificate issued by CSA Group. Offices sit across North America and Australia, with the corporate office in Huntsville, Alabama, and open roles are posted within IDEX Corporation.

before.name: Aquarius Spectrum
before.description: Fixed acoustic leak monitoring sensors for municipal water networks

paragraphs: Aquarius Spectrum sells acoustic leak detection systems that let water utilities find and prevent leaks. The stated aim is cutting non-revenue water and putting resources where they matter. The products are meant to suit water networks of any pipe material and size.

Sensors take a daily audio sample and send it to a cloud server for analysis. Every two coupled sensors are then correlated, and when the same noise turns up in the same location an alert gives the exact position of the leak. The AQS-SYS platform pairs those sensors with algorithms, big data analytics and CAT-M or NB-IoT connectivity. Accelerometers fit externally on hydrants above ground and on pressure and air valves below. A hydrophone covers large transmission lines of 24 inches and above, plus plastic and PVC pipe. Where continuous monitoring is not wanted, mobile products let a utility survey large areas instead.

Alongside the hardware the company sells what it calls Human-as-a-Service, described as ongoing human support, expertise and system updates. AQS states that it is a company of the Aliaxis Group. It reports receiving ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification. Published case studies include the national agency that manages Singapore's water loop.

before.name: 2NDNATURE
before.description: Stormwater program and MS4 compliance software for municipalities

paragraphs: 2NDNATURE sells stormwater software built on GIS, aimed at streamlining compliance, asset tracking and reporting. Buyers fall into two camps, those tackling MS4 permit requirements and those advancing corporate water stewardship. Two products carry that work, 2NFORM and Rainsteward, both pitched at streamlining compliance and showing measurable results.

2NFORM is organized around municipal permit programs, covering post-construction, industrial and commercial, and illicit discharge detection and elimination. In Oceanside it was connected to the city's existing Esri-based GIS and met local security and IT standards. For longer-range planning the company built a Stormwater Asset Management Model that serves as a decision-making tool. Fed with the storm sewer system and local costs, it lets a city explore how twenty years of asset management would affect the health of that system. Rainsteward points the other way, at owners trying to cut costs and get more value out of stormwater investments.

The customers shown are city stormwater programs; Oceanside had nine separate systems tracking inspections and compliance tasks before it changed course. Salinas is described as a Phase I MS4 with a population exceeding 150,000. That city worked with 2NDNATURE to develop a comprehensive Asset Improvement Plan. Private owners appear too: a real estate company called Reveler implemented Rainsteward in a series of six steps.

quote.text: Mapping your storm sewer system can feel overwhelming, but strategic approaches can make the effort manageable.

before.name: InfoSense
before.description: SL-RAT acoustic sewer line assessment tools for municipal sewer agencies - exhibited at WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: InfoSense sells the equipment, software and services that let a city work out which sewer pipes actually need cleaning before crews are sent out. The centrepiece is a handheld acoustic device that scores blockage conditions in small diameter gravity sewer lines.

A transmitter goes on one open manhole and a receiver on the next. Within a few minutes the display returns a rating from zero to ten showing whether the pipe is clear or obstructed. Nothing touches the flow and nobody has to enter a confined space. The company reports that two people can cover fifty to sixty segments in a day. Readings feed a companion platform that records, organises and maps the results. Data can be pushed out to mapping and spreadsheet tools already in use.

Buyers are public works departments and utilities moving away from cleaning on a fixed calendar toward cleaning based on measured condition. The company states that more than 1,350 utilities have used the tool. One published case study covers a small town serving just under ten thousand people. That town is reported to have cut its cleaning workload by more than half.

quote.text: Turn Hours into Minutes and Dollars into Sense

provenance.quote: We help municipalities take control of their sewer maintenance with equipment, software, and services that turn invisible conditions into actionable assessments.
The SL-RAT is a portable acoustic device engineered to assess blockage conditions in small-diameter gravity sewer lines.

before.name: 120Water
before.description: Lead service line inventories, sampling, and compliance software - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: 120Water sells compliance software to public water utilities and to the state agencies that oversee them. The company describes one shared system that standardizes water data and requirements into reporting and community communications. The argument for it is that utilities and agencies otherwise track assets and water quality across disconnected tools, which hurts data integrity.

The platform gathers the programs and data a team needs to manage compliance from start to finish. That includes asset records and service line inventories, sampling schedules, lab results, resident communications, and program reporting. Programs run on it include service line inventories, monitoring, school and childcare sampling, backflow, consumer request sampling, and statewide 3Ts programs. It is built to fit an existing data ecosystem, with lab integrations and APIs for syncing locations, assets, and records. Most utility and state clients onboard in weeks, with the company handling data migration, configuration, and training.

Public water systems, state drinking water programs, schools, childcare facilities, and local governments are named as the customers. The company states that every module is built with current security standards and role-based permissions meant to meet or exceed state and federal program requirements. Its stated mission is to protect public health by giving communities confidence in their water. The chief executive came from the growth equity firm Edison Partners, which the about page names as the lead investor.

before.name: VODA.ai
before.description: AI pipe-failure prediction for main replacement planning - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: VODA.ai sells decision support software to water utilities. The point is helping engineers decide which pipes to replace, assess, monitor or investigate next.

Projects start from data a utility already keeps, such as GIS records, pipe attributes, historical break records, work orders and service line information. Machine learning then flags pipes with an elevated likelihood of failure, including ones that have never broken. Utilities do not need clean records to begin. Initial model outputs, risk scores and prioritized watch lists are often available within three to six months. The same approach supports lead service line programs, sorting likely galvanized lines and prioritizing field verification before replacement work.

The company is Boston-based and was founded in 2017. It says it has worked in 31 states and eight countries and analyzed more than a million miles of pipe. Executives from 78 water utilities at the Smart Water Summit picked it as best smart water solution. Published case studies include lead compliance work in Rock Hill, South Carolina.

paragraphs: Banyan Water sells water management software to commercial customers who want control over what their properties consume. Irrigation is the piece the company points to first, claiming reductions of 40 to 60 percent while the landscape stays healthy.

Watering schedules are set from local weather, property size, plant life, and the type of irrigation system installed. A patented leak detection feature monitors irrigation water and can shut the system off automatically when a problem appears. Indoors, real-time monitoring is meant to catch leaks before damage occurs or an unexpected bill arrives. Submeters on individual tenants let property managers bill back by actual volume rather than by an even split.

The company says its systems are installed at over 1,000 properties in the United States, across multifamily, office, retail, hospitality, and mixed use buildings. Reported savings are checked against the customer's utility bills. A mobile app lets clients see information about water use from a phone.

paragraphs: In-Situ sells water quality, level and flow monitoring solutions built for reliable performance and accurate data. The company says its instrumentation and software work together to deliver decision-quality data in real time.

The line covers monitoring groundwater, surface water, wastewater or drinking water. Hardware runs from industrial-grade online analyzers to portable monitors and flexible communication options. VuLink telemetry and HydroVu data services are offered so that data access from anywhere is easy and affordable.

Application pages include continuous groundwater monitoring, measuring water level and water quality over time at local or regional scales. Others cover remote monitoring for harmful algal blooms, for quick response and improved trend analysis. Flood monitoring is framed as the continuous measurement of water level and flow for flood control management. before.name: SmartCover Systems
before.description: Remote sewer level and overflow monitoring for municipal collection systems - exhibited at WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: SmartCover sells remote monitoring and controls for sewer, lift stations and stormwater infrastructure. The company describes the offering as turning real-time remote infrastructure data into insights for utility customers who want to minimize OpEx and reduce CapEx. Stated uses include overflow prevention, cleaning schedules, I&I identification, and chemical optimization.

The pages present satellite communication as what keeps the system visible. Alarms and notifications are described as giving advance notice so staff can prepare and respond. Installation is described as needing no confined space entry, with the work done in shop. A mobile app is offered, with system insights available wherever the user is.

A published case study covers the City of Kelowna in British Columbia. That city is described as using the technology for overflow prevention, optimization of high frequency cleaning, and ongoing I&I studies. Other departments in the city are described as using it for H2S monitoring, leachate at the solid waste facility, and stream level monitoring.

paragraphs: Forerunner sells software it calls a geospatial intelligence layer. The platform unifies geospatial data, field operations, and AI-powered workflows in one place. Local government is a core buyer, with compliance work across stormwater, floodplain, and code enforcement programs. The company also markets to energy and infrastructure operators handling inspections across active sites and assets.

At the base sits a map-first view holding every asset, permit parcel, violation, and environmental layer. On top of it run configurable workflows for inspections, permits, violations, and grant tracking. Inspection findings then generate corrective actions, and permit deadlines trigger notifications. The company says adoption brings no rip-and-replace projects and no major workflow disruptions. It claims teams are up and running in weeks.

Published case studies name the Puerto Rico Planning Board, which the company says replaced paper forms and spreadsheets for field inspections and code compliance. Another states that Lee County saves approximately 16 hours of staff time per week. A further case study describes Ponce Inlet centralizing National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System workflows to reclaim 10 or more hours per week.
