before.name: Muni-Link
before.description: Cloud utility billing, payments, and service order software for municipal water and wastewater utilities - exhibited at GFOA 2026

paragraphs: Muni-Link sells cloud-based utility billing software for water and wastewater utilities. The platform brings customer accounts, billing, payments, service orders, and customer communications together in one system. Readings, estimates, reports, calculations, and printing are completed on a single page, and irregularities are flagged for review before bills go out.

Staff can view customer account details and usage history, dispatch service orders, take payments, manage delinquency, and send notifications from a single screen. Service orders are dispatched and tracked between office teams and technicians in real time, with updates logged on customer accounts. Automated notifications go to customers by phone call, email, or text. The software integrates with asset management, accounting, GIS, and AMR/AMI systems.

Muni-Link says it helps municipal utilities, utility authorities, water districts, and regulated utilities manage their accounts. The software is described as built for cities, towns, and the people who serve them. Unlimited support is built into the subscription fee at no extra cost. Muni-Link is headquartered in central Pennsylvania. Neptune Technology Group owns the company.

before.name: Aquanuity, Inc.
before.description: AquaTwin digital twin software for water and sewer hydraulic modeling, surge analysis, and asset management, sold to water utilities and engineering consultants - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: Aquanuity sells water, wastewater and stormwater modeling and asset management software that runs inside Esri ArcGIS Pro. Buyers are utilities and the engineering consultants working on their systems across the asset lifecycle.

AquaTwin Water models a distribution network so users can forecast demand, tune tank and pump operation, cut energy use and look into water quality problems. AquaTwin Sewer covers planning, design and analysis of stormwater, sanitary and combined sewer systems. That product is built on the EPA SWMM 5 engine. An extension named ATLive ties a model to SCADA so it can run against live readings from sensors and control systems. AquaTwin Asset turns condition and risk work into prioritized, costed capital improvement projects.

The company publishes benchmark papers, one of which reports its sewer solver outperforming the SWMM5 dynamic wave method by at least a factor of eight. It also states that the two-dimensional module did well in the UK Environment Agency hydraulic model benchmark test cases. Aquanuity frames its purpose as helping achieve environmentally, economically and socially sustainable water and wastewater infrastructure.

before.name: Baseform
before.description: Network data analytics software for water utilities covering leakage, infiltration, energy use and capital planning - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: Baseform makes software for networked water infrastructures, sold to utilities as analytics and planning tools. The product is presented as end-to-end software for the operational management of a water or wastewater system.

It continuously tracks and reconciles utility SCADA, GIS, billing, AMI and other data sources. One module handles event detection, DMA management, component analysis, non-revenue water reporting and infiltration tracking. Another covers failure and condition prediction, risk exposure, renewal planning and capital project generation. A billing module manages meters, consumption, revenue, under-registration and meter changeout. Network hydraulics are factored in continuously rather than treated as an afterthought.

The results are meant to reach everyone from the technicians who generate the analyses to field crews and top level executives. The stated approach is making better use of data that utilities and cities already collect daily. The company dates its inception to January 2015. It states that it is 100% owned and managed by its founders. One example given on the product page is a Texas public utility using the predictive analytics against a yearly rise in pipe breaks.

paragraphs: Envirosight makes inspection equipment for the pipes that carry sewage and stormwater underground. That equipment is sold to cities and to the contractors who do the same work for them.

before.name: Electro Scan
before.description: Machine-based pipe defect and leak assessment for municipal sewer and water - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: Electro Scan sells leak detection and lead pipe location work for water and sewer systems. The company says municipal sewer utilities and sewer contractors use it to pin down the location, measurement and flow of defects inside a pipe before a repair or replacement job.

The method rests on a simple claim: pipe defects that leak water also leak electricity, so a defect shows up whether or not it happens to be leaking during the inspection. A low voltage conductivity probe travels through the pipe at 45 to 60 feet per minute, locating and measuring defects as it goes. Crews can then create summary and detail level reports for a team to review. The flagship probe is built for gravity mains between 6 and 30 inches in diameter, and the company says agencies and contractors use it worldwide.

Electro Scan lists ISO 9001:2015 certification for quality management systems. Its case studies page includes a North American benchmark study comparing closed-circuit television inspection with focused electrode leak location on gravity sewer mains. Other write-ups describe a Florida utility dealing with excessive inflow and infiltration in its gravity collection system.

paragraphs: KETOS sells water quality monitoring as an integrated service rather than as standalone instruments. The KETOS SHIELD reports water quality data in real time across dozens of parameters, and the KETOS WAVE reports flow, pressure and volume. Sensor readings are aggregated in a data warehouse that feeds reporting, alerts and predictive analytics for water operators.

The platform is sold with no capital expenditure and an annual service fee in place of equipment purchase. Connectivity options include LoRa, WiFi and cellular, and the platform connects to public data and existing SCADA systems. Reports and alerts are offered as configurable and out of the box, without separate analytics staff.

Municipal, industrial and agricultural applications are each named on the site, and each carries an average customer rating. Case studies name a Fortune 500 consumer goods manufacturer that monitors three locations on a daily and by shift basis. Another case study describes a Midwest power plant that needed regular water testing for compliance.

before.name: LeakZon
before.description: AI water loss and non-revenue water analytics that detect leaks, bursts and consumption anomalies from utility meter and SCADA data - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: LeakZon, established 2023, develops an analytical solution that reduces the water loss rate, also known as Non-Revenue Water. It collects and analyzes raw AMR, GIS maps, CIS and other relevant environmental data. Proprietary AI tools optimize the District Metered Areas and detect water anomalies such as leaks, metering inaccuracies, unauthorized consumption and abnormal usage.

Continuous analysis of meter and SCADA data flags leaks, bursts and night-flow anomalies as soon as they appear. The platform creates virtual DMAs that split a water network into virtual zones without physical works or new sensors. An onboarding wizard gathers data from GIS, meters, SCADA, billing and other sources and builds a digital picture of the network. Once onboarded, the platform monitors the network around the clock and turns each anomaly into a managed issue. The platform follows the AWWA M36 water audit methodology, classifying every drop from system input volume down to revenue and non-revenue water.

The homepage states that LeakZon serves the whole water ecosystem. Utilities are the audience for the alerts, dispatching crews to the locations the AI pinpoints. Water service providers are a second named segment, with LeakZon offered to them as a value-added service. LeakZon already operates across the United States, including Texas, California, Illinois, Pennsylvania and Florida.

before.name: BlueConduit
before.description: Machine learning lead service line inventory and prediction for water utilities - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: BlueConduit sells predictive modeling tools to water systems that need to manage risk and make data-driven decisions about their distribution assets. The customers are municipalities and water utilities.

One product builds community-specific models that pinpoint high-risk lead and galvanized service lines, which lets a utility classify its inventory and prioritize replacements. Another scores every main segment in a network for likelihood and consequence of failure. A third uses statistical models to confirm the absence of lead in a water system. The company says model processes, important features, and performance metrics are always shared with customers. Output is integrated with Esri ArcGIS.

The work started at the University of Michigan, where faculty and student researchers saw a use for data science in removing toxic lead from the water supply. In Flint the company used predictive analytics to identify where to dig for lead service lines. A published case study describes Des Moines Water Works classifying unknown service lines and reducing uncertainty by 75% in six months. BlueConduit cites ongoing relationships with EPA and state regulators. Its stated mission is to empower communities to prioritize health and sustainability through data science.

before.name: Ovarro
before.description: Leak detection, RTUs and network monitoring for water utilities

paragraphs: Ovarro builds monitoring, control and data technology for organizations managing critical assets across water, oil and gas, broadcast, process, energy and transportation. The hardware range runs to remote telemetry units, acoustic microphones, data loggers, leak noise loggers, correlators and flow meters.

SCOPE, the company's enterprise SCADA and telemetry system, monitors and controls a diverse range of assets in real time. Analytics products named BurstDetect, BlockageDetect and PumpInsight watch pumps and work to prevent sewer bursts and blockages. Consultancy sits alongside the products, with technical directors and analysts specialising in asset management, leakage and demand, and network optimisation.

Published case studies lean heavily on water utilities, among them LeakNavigator work described as saving millions of litres for Thames Water. Another describes a SCADA deployment enabling real-time monitoring of more than 2,000 assets, with gains in efficiency, leakage detection and planning. The company reports more than 250 experienced colleagues and over 70 certified channel partners around the world. It dates its origins to industrial automation for the steel industry in the North of England forty years ago.

before.name: Klir
before.description: Permitting, compliance, and workflow software for water utilities - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: Klir sells compliance and operations software built for drinking water and wastewater utilities. The argument for it is that administration and paperwork take up more than half the working time of utility scientists, engineers and operators. The platform holds that work as centralized, accessible data in one place.

On the drinking water side it manages SDWA permit adherence from start to finish. For wastewater it manages NPDES permit adherence. Pretreatment teams track industrial user details, permits and data. Staff reach it anywhere through a cloud platform with mobile inspections and field data entry. It is described as configurable and compatible with a Microsoft Azure stack alongside LIMS, GIS and SCADA.

Co-founders David Lynch and Elaine Kelly met while working with European drinking water and wastewater utilities and regulators. The company says large water and wastewater organizations in the United States, Canada and Australia now use it to centralize and automate compliance reporting. The team has grown past 60 people across the United States, Canada, Brazil and Ireland. The company lists SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001 and NIST compliance, and sells directly, through the Microsoft Azure Marketplace or on cooperative contracts.

before.name: RedZone Robotics
before.description: Robotic sewer inspection and condition assessment services - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: RedZone Robotics sells robotic sewer inspection, large-diameter cleaning, and asset management for underground wastewater infrastructure. Robots carrying cameras and sensors are sent into pipes to perform pipeline and sewer assessments. The data collected is uploaded to cloud-based software that the customer accesses to assess an entire pipeline and decide on maintenance.

The pages date the company to 1987 and say it pivoted in 2003 to focus exclusively on wastewater, beginning work with the City of Pittsburgh on a tool for inspecting large-diameter pipe. Later development produced Vertue, described as a vertical manhole inspection unit providing customers with comprehensive asset data. Services listed run from small and mid-sized pipe to large-diameter MSI inspection, siphons, and interceptors.

Buyers named on the pages are asset managers at large and small municipalities and agencies, along with regional and national engineering firms. The employment page adds contractors and engineering firms across North America to that list.

before.name: SwiftComply
before.description: Regulatory compliance software for water utilities covering backflow prevention, stormwater MS4, industrial pretreatment and fats, oils and grease programs - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: SwiftComply sells compliance management software for water, wastewater, and stormwater utilities, covering Backflow Prevention, Stormwater, Industrial Pretreatment, and FOG management. It replaces spreadsheet and paper based compliance tracking with one system for reporting, follow-up, and enforcement. Live dashboards show compliance rates, outstanding items, and trends across programs. Every inspection, report, and follow-up is timestamped and stored for a state audit or permit review.

These pages say the software is used by municipal water and wastewater utilities, public works departments, and water/sewer districts. Named customers include cities and counties such as Houston, Atlanta, Fort Worth, Charlotte Water, Dallas, Tampa, and Honolulu. The pages say 700+ organizations across North America run compliance programs on it.

Each solution is priced separately, typically as a one-time implementation fee plus an annual subscription. Backflow programs can also choose a tester-pay model, where a per-test fee is passed to testers instead of the utility funding the subscription. The software is available through cooperative purchasing vehicles such as Omnia Partners, NASPO, and Carahsoft, which many public agencies can use without running a separate competitive bid.

before.name: ASTERRA
before.description: Satellite-based leak detection and underground pipe assessment - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: ASTERRA sells insight into what lies beneath the ground, produced without breaking ground using patented algorithms and artificial intelligence to detect leaks. Water and wastewater utilities use it for leak detection to reduce non-revenue water and for analysis of potable and wastewater systems. The same approach maps excess soil moisture near or under dams, levees, roads, railways and mining operations.

The company images a customer's system with polarimetric synthetic aperture radar to sense and evaluate soil moisture. The same regions are revisited every few days or weeks as needed to monitor vast expanses. Results land in EO Discover, described as the repository for all insights from a customer's ASTERRA projects. There, detections, hotspots and network risk appear in a single view. MasterPlan scores pipe segments that show non-surfacing leaks and analyzes leak clusters over time. EarthWorks uses synthetic aperture radar to detect soil moisture up to 10 feet below the surface.

Field crews log investigation results, leak location and other data using U-Collect or the Esri ArcGIS Field Maps app. Within five minutes that reporting is available in EO Discover. The company ties EarthWorks, MasterPlan and Recover to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. MasterPlan is available in the Advise level of an ASTERRA Recover subscription.

before.name: Aquatic Informatics (Veralto)
before.description: Water data management (AQUARIUS, WaterTrax) for utilities and environmental agencies - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: Aquatic Informatics makes water data management software covering the full water cycle, sold to utilities, cities and monitoring agencies. The pitch is consolidating scattered data sources so an agency can report against regulations with an audit trail behind it.

Aquarius covers environmental monitoring data from acquisition through management to web based publication and decision support. WaterTrax centralizes sampling schedules, remote data collection and compliance reporting for municipalities. Linko handles fats, oils and grease programs, industrial pretreatment and hauled waste records. Tokay is aimed at cross connection control and backflow prevention programs. Hach WIMS stores process data in a central database that provides an audit trail and preserves historical records.

A module named HydroCorrect applies machine learning inside Aquarius to speed up reaction to environmental events. The company says Hach handed it the WIMS platform in 2021, citing more than twenty years of experience in water data management systems. Aquarius Cloud is offered as a fully managed service hosted on Amazon Web Services.

before.name: Placemetry
before.description: AI street-imagery analysis: pavement condition, sign inventory, and blight for public works and code enforcement - exhibited at Smart Cities Connect 2026

paragraphs: Placemetry drives a city and captures photos from the public right-of-way, then analyzes properties and roadways with AI so departments can get ahead of problems rather than react to them. Each vehicle is equipped with three high-resolution cameras, one facing forward and one facing to each side, capturing street-level imagery in a single drive. Forward-facing cameras deliver per-segment pavement condition, an asset inventory, and safety screening in a single pass.

Side cameras capture a wide view of the public right-of-way in one pass, including properties, yards, sidewalks, trees, and vegetation. The same dataset feeds Code Enforcement, Economic Development, and Forestry & Parks. All imagery is captured from the public right-of-way, faces and license plates are blurred, and the city owns the data.

One cadence is a single citywide survey with no subscription required. Another is a quarterly or bi-annual citywide sweep in which Placemetry teams drive every street and the AI scores properties. A third option puts cameras on city vehicles the city already operates, so garbage trucks and street sweepers capture passive citywide coverage. Delivery runs through direct API integrations, standard spreadsheet downloads, or a secure web app, with REST API Endpoints and Webhooks.

before.name: Acusensus
before.description: AI cameras detecting phone use, seatbelt, and speed violations for road authorities - exhibited at ITS America 2026

paragraphs: Acusensus sells automated traffic enforcement systems to the road authorities and police agencies that are trying to cut deaths and injuries on the road network. Its main product, Heads-Up, detects drivers illegally using a mobile phone and captures evidence intended to stand up in a prosecution.

The same camera pass picks up other behaviours, so one deployment can address seatbelt non-compliance and speed measured at a point or averaged over a distance. A companion product sends live alerts to officers working the roadside. Assessment happens at the roadside, and images of drivers who are not offending are discarded almost immediately. Evidence that is kept is encrypted so that only the customer agency can open it.

The company says the government of New South Wales used its technology in a program enforcing against illegal phone use by drivers. Its list of delivered work includes an Arkansas speed enforcement program covering work zones. Acusensus also reports ISO accreditation for occupational health and safety, quality, environmental and information security management systems.

Acusensus Real-Time provides alerts to police officers of drivers using a phone, speeding, not wearing a seatbelt or on an automatic number plate recognition wanted list.

paragraphs: Miovision sells traffic data collection tools meant to give planners the accurate, verifiable data their mobility plans depend on. It also sells detection equipment that improves signal performance by responding to real-world road user demand, from bicycles to articulated trucks. Its Opticom line clears the path for emergency fleets without re-timing entire corridors.

Portable devices capture comprehensive multimodal count data including cars, trucks, pedestrians and bikes. A newer optimization product replaces manual five-year retiming cycles with iterative, objective-based optimization that the company says cuts manual effort by up to half. Engineers compare plans side-by-side, validate against industry standards, and push updates directly to field controllers without manual data re-entry.

The company says that since 2005 it has had 2,000 customers in 68 countries and 13,000 cities, with 30 billion vehicles and 1.5 billion pedestrians counted. It lists more than 300 detection customers in North America. Detroit partnered with Miovision to upgrade over 600 intersections. In San Rafael, police and fire vehicles now receive signal priority at 53 intersections.

paragraphs: Miovision sells traffic data collection tools meant to give planners the accurate, verifiable data their mobility plans depend on. It also sells detection equipment that improves signal performance by responding to real-world road user demand, from bicycles to articulated trucks. Its Opticom line clears the path for emergency fleets without re-timing entire corridors.

Portable devices capture comprehensive multimodal count data including cars, trucks, pedestrians and bikes. A newer optimization product replaces manual five-year retiming cycles with iterative, objective-based optimization that the company says cuts manual effort by up to half. Engineers compare plans side-by-side, validate against industry standards, and push updates directly to field controllers without manual data re-entry.

The company says that since 2005 it has had 2,000 customers in 68 countries and 13,000 cities, with 30 billion vehicles and 1.5 billion pedestrians counted. It lists more than 300 detection customers in North America. Detroit partnered with Miovision to upgrade over 600 intersections. In San Rafael, police and fire vehicles now receive signal priority at 53 intersections.

roles.title: Key Account Executive - Central Government, Infrastructure & Public Safety - Belgium

paragraphs: Cyclomedia sells geospatial data built from street-level imagery, lidar point clouds, and aerial data covering public space. Public authorities are a core market, using it to manage streets, buildings, and public assets. Utility and energy providers use it to plan, inspect, and manage their networks.

Street Smart, the company's viewer, brings 360 degree imagery, lidar, and map layers into one browser-based workspace. From the desk, users measure distances along facades, pavements, and openings. Automated analysis detects pavement defects, surface types, and deterioration in high-resolution imagery. Property valuation is another stated use, supported by current visual evidence and measurements. Open integrations and APIs connect the data to existing GIS and asset management systems.

The company says it has worked in geospatial capture and visualisation for more than 40 years with public authorities across Europe and beyond. Specialised capture vehicles survey cities and regions throughout the year. Routes are coordinated with local authorities to limit disruption. Its case studies page lists a digital twin created for the London Borough of Harrow from street imagery and lidar.

quote.text: Shift more work from the field to the office by using Street Smart and work more efficiently.

paragraphs: Nexar sells dash cams for cars, paired with a phone app that saves and backs up the footage. The range is sorted by how much of the car is covered, from front only to front, cabin and rear. Recording runs from Full HD to 4K, and models with built-in LTE send alerts and live video without a paired phone.

Pages for each camera name the drivers it is for: rideshare and delivery drivers, parents with kids in the back seat, and daily commuters. The smallest model is aimed at compact-car owners, parents passing a car down to a teen driver, and first-time buyers. The 4K model is pitched at long-distance commuters, rideshare drivers, and owners of newer or higher-value cars. Live alerts, vehicle tracking and cloud backup sit behind a subscription the pages price at $9.99 a month.

quote.text: Nexar is more than a dashcam. It watches, warns, and proves so you never face the road alone.

before.name: i-Probe
before.description: Connected-vehicle road condition monitoring and pavement analytics for DOTs and counties (SoftBank-backed JV)

paragraphs: i-Probe monitors road conditions with connected vehicles, which the pages define as vehicles that use bidirectional communications to address road conditions, safety, system efficiency, or mobility on roadways. The pages address road management agencies and describe the offering as more economical, rapid, and consistent road condition monitoring. The technology leverages factory-installed sensors already built into later-model production vehicles, developed in partnership with Honda Motors, and requires no aftermarket equipment.

Connected vehicles collect road roughness data either through crowdsourcing or through a single-vehicle service. That roughness data is processed under an i-Probe algorithm to identify pavement distresses and severity, and the outputs are mapped and tabulated in a cloud dashboard. Distress identification and classification are automated and paired with video verification. Reasons given for choosing the service include results correlated to IRI. Wide-area monitoring of an entire road network is listed among those reasons.
The page names county and municipal public works agencies as one group served. Pavement maintenance service providers are named as the other group served.

paragraphs: Rhythm Engineering sells In|Sync, an adaptive traffic signal control system that the company says is deployed at more than 3,000 intersections nationwide. The product line also includes CYCLOPS, a vehicle recognition system powered by AI algorithms. A third product, code|GREEN, combines vehicle detection, data collection, timing plan generation, and deployment.

Rhythm Engineering was founded in 2005 by Dr. Reggie Chandra, a traffic engineer who worked in the public sector. In|Sync has since been installed in 31 states and by 140 public agencies. Testimonials on the homepage come from a City Council Member in San Diego, CA and a Principal Traffic Engineer in West des Moines, IA.

paragraphs: StreetLight sells transportation analytics built on a big data platform rather than on field counts. The platform covers roadway volumes, transportation modeling, congestion management and safety studies, with AADT and origin-destination metrics. Delivery runs three ways: self-serve software, bulk data through an API, and custom services from a data science team.

Products are grouped by industry, and the groupings named on the site are government, business, consultants and academics. Government users are pitched planning, operations and climate work; business users are pitched retail, fuel and electric vehicle charging applications. StreetLight dates its founding to 2011 and became part of the professional services firm Jacobs in 2022. The platform is named StreetLight InSight, and the about page describes bicycle, pedestrian, bus and rail metrics added to its core measures.

before.name: Derq
before.description: AI intersection safety and V2X analytics for DOTs and cities - exhibited at ITS America 2026

paragraphs: Derq builds intelligent transportation systems for safer roads. It sells to agencies, helping them improve safety and optimize traffic flow for all road users.

The platform detects, tracks, classifies, and predicts road user behavior in real time, and the company says it does so accurately in all weather and lighting conditions. It is compatible with a wide range of sensors, including video detection, CCTV and radar, as well as traffic controllers and V2X technologies. Edge-based traffic detection covers vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists. Analytics deliver safety insights, traffic performance data, near-miss insights, and ATSPMs. V2X applications are aimed at preventing collisions between vehicles and vulnerable road users.

Derq describes itself as an MIT spinoff founded in 2016. It says its technology is live across the United States, Canada, and the GCC. The company reports more than 20 patents. It states that it is SOC 2 Type II compliant. The site also announces that Derq was named a winner of the USDOT Intersection Safety Challenge.

The platform detects, tracks, classifies, and predicts road user behavior in real time, and the company says it does so accurately in all weather and lighting conditions. It is compatible with a wide range of sensors, including video detection, CCTV and radar, as well as traffic controllers and V2X technologies. Edge-based traffic detection covers vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists. Analytics deliver safety insights, traffic performance data, near-miss insights, and ATSPMs. V2X applications are aimed at preventing collisions between vehicles and vulnerable road users.

Derq describes itself as an MIT spinoff founded in 2016. It says its technology is live across the United States, Canada, and the GCC. The company reports more than 20 patents. It states that it is SOC 2 Type II compliant. The site also announces that Derq was named a winner of the USDOT Intersection Safety Challenge.

before.description: iPhone-lidar sidewalk and curb-ramp inspection for ADA transition plans, ArcGIS-integrated; 120+ munis - exhibited at ITS America 2026

paragraphs: DeepWalk sells automated sidewalk inspection software that uses iPhone LiDAR to identify condition and access issues. Work is planned, inspected, analyzed and implemented on one platform. Projects range from small residential work to city-wide deployments.

Crews scan sidewalk and curb ramps with the LiDAR scanners in iPhone Pros through the mobile app. An automated measurement system then inspects the scans for condition and accessibility issues. Data comes back in the web app and in ArcGIS. There, inspections are managed, conditions reviewed and work orders created for improvements. A higher plan is aimed at large evaluations and long-term planning projects that require slope analysis.

All plans include the full capability of the mobile app, which is downloaded from the Apple App Store. The site describes a pilot in which Edina, MN, got faster, more efficient data collection. Another story says Genoa, IL, went from data collection to program implementation and earned statewide recognition.

before.name: HAAS Alert
before.description: Safety Cloud digital alerting for DOT, fire and public works fleets - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026, ITS America 2026
before.source: competitor sweep; IAFC FRI 2026; ITS America 2026

paragraphs: HAAS Alert sells a collision prevention service that sends real-time digital alerts warning drivers about nearby emergency vehicles and roadway hazards. Its customers are fleets that work at the roadside, including tow trucks, utility vehicles, waste management trucks, school buses and snowplows.

The system is wired to a vehicle's warning light bar or master switch, so alerting begins when crews turn on their lights and stops when they turn them off. Motorists install nothing, because alerts are broadcast directly to the navigation platforms they already use. Fleets can activate the service through three primary methods, depending on their existing setup. The company says drivers get up to 30 seconds of advance warning to slow down and move over.

The company traces its start to 2015, when co-founder and CEO Cory Hohs was almost struck by an ambulance on the road. He co-founded the business with Noah Levens and Jigar Patel. Its timeline notes that the United States Department of Homeland Security awarded $1.1 million toward development for digital alerting. It also states that digital alerting was codified and funded in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

paragraphs: StreetSaver is pavement and asset management software, described on its home page as tools to plan, forecast, budget and report. The home page says the software helps cities, counties, and private institutions manage and maintain pavements, roadways, and other infrastructure assets. It is delivered as web based software reachable across a variety of platforms.

Listed capabilities include projecting treatments and costs up to 30 years into the future. The site counts over 90 reports and graphs available to users. Condition data can be collected through a mobile option. The software also extends to non-pavement assets such as traffic signs and curb ramps.

A separate product page sells a PCI distress identification manual covering flexible and rigid pavements. That manual describes each pavement distress type used in StreetSaver and sets criteria for three levels of severity. The home page carries a copyright line naming the Metropolitan Transportation Commission.

before.name: GoodVision
before.description: Video-based traffic survey and analytics software for road authorities

paragraphs: GoodVision sells traffic analysis software to transportation professionals, who use it to collect, analyze and act on traffic data taken from video footage or live camera streams. Its main platform, Video Insights, extracts data from videos in place of manual collection and uses AI to analyze traffic and automate model calibration.

A second product works on live feeds rather than uploads, analysing camera streams on the fly and passing traffic data to third-party systems such as traffic management systems and controllers. The incident detection module recognises user-defined traffic events, flags them and reports them to traffic management centre controllers. At intersections and roundabouts it counts volumes and derives parameters such as speed, gaps between vehicles, dwell time and passage time. Finished reports can be edited, regenerated and exported in Excel, CSV or custom formats.

The company describes the same monitoring applied to bridges and tunnels, where the goal is to prevent congestion and catch accidents early. Alongside direct sales, GoodVision runs a partner program and says it is seeking global distribution and service partners.

before.name: Deighton Associates

paragraphs: Deighton sells infrastructure asset management software to transportation agencies and other public owners of roads and bridges. The product is dTIMS, the Deighton Total Infrastructure Management System. Roads, bridges, facilities, and other asset classes are managed within it.

The suite starts with business analytics for life cycle cost analysis, performance modeling, and scenario planning. An operations module manages work orders, service requests, crew scheduling, inventory, and day-to-day maintenance activities. A field-ready app handles inspections and work execution online or offline, keeping condition records current. An environmental module scores maintenance strategies using Global Warming Potential metrics. Agencies of any size can run it in the cloud or on premises.

The company says the dTIMS suite has been used by agencies in more than 40 countries over four decades. It gives its headquarters as Canada and Ireland, with implementations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Africa, and the Middle East. Published case studies include adding bridge management to an existing pavement system at Arkansas DOT. Deighton also announced ISO 27001 certification for information security management.

paragraphs: Citylogix sells municipal asset and work order management software, pitched at communities of every size. It also collects the data that feeds the software, driving streets with LiDAR and 360-degree imaging to map road conditions and right-of-way assets.

Inside the software, work orders are tied to the assets themselves and travel from the office to the crew and back. Machine learning grades pavement distress and turns it into heatmaps of the worst stretches. Sidewalk and ADA ramp condition assessment is offered alongside the road work. Budget and capital planning tools are meant to help a public works director justify what gets funded. Resident service requests drop into the same work order queue.

The customers are municipalities across North America. The company reports miles under management in 40 states, four provinces and one territory. It also counts ramps assessed for ADA and AODA compliance among its results. A recent announcement describes a partnership with NIRA Dynamics for continuous, IRI-based road monitoring using survey vehicles. The contact block lists an address on Salem Street in Wakefield, Massachusetts.

before.name: Builterra
before.description: Construction contract administration software covering quantity take-off, bidding, field inspection, and payment certification for municipalities and civil engineering consultants - exhibited at NACE 2026

paragraphs: Builterra is a civil engineering software provider that sells construction contract administration software, and it was founded in 2014. Its buyers are public and private civil infrastructure teams.

The platform runs the whole workflow, from design quantity take-offs and cost estimating through bid preparation, analysis, and processing, then field inspection reporting and progress payment certification. Take-offs and real-time cost estimates can be produced inside CAD or in a bid preparation portal, priced against historic figures. In the field, the app connects to the bid and captures construction progress and photos, all geo-located. Monthly payment certificates are generated from that data.

The company names AECOM, WSP, Stantec, Parsons, SNC Lavalin, and Defense Construction Canada among its clients, along with large municipalities across Canada and the United States. It was started by Jeff Lyons and Chris Stebbing. The company reports more than five billion dollars in progress payment certificates processed. It also reports over a million inspection photos documented and mapped.

before.name: Econolite
before.description: Traffic signal controllers, cabinets, and intersection management systems

paragraphs: Econolite sells traffic management equipment and services to transportation agencies responsible for roadway efficiency. The catalog includes traffic control cabinets in standard configurations and to unique specifications. It sells traffic signal controllers for intersection management. Detection sensors cover vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians. The company is also a licensed electrical contractor doing traffic signal and ITS maintenance and repair.

Its cabinet designs draw on features of Caltrans, NEMA and ITS cabinets. The Advanced Traffic Control Cabinet uses high-speed serial communications. Its standard configuration allows up to 32 signal outputs and 120 detection inputs. A separate line covers NEMA TS1 and TS2 cabinets built for traffic applications. Battery backup keeps signals operating during a power disruption.

Agencies can book an on-site session with the company to review cabinet performance and specifications. Recent site news names a distributor for the Northwest United States. It also reports European Union certification for a radar detection product. Another item describes adaptive traffic control in Hamburg with Umovity and PTV Group.

before.name: Flow Labs
before.description: Probe-data traffic signal performance and safety software for DOTs - exhibited at ITS America 2026

paragraphs: Flow Labs sells software that transportation agencies, engineering firms, and commercial fleets use to work on road safety and traffic flow. The company says the software requires no new hardware to be installed. Instead it takes real-time traffic data and turns it into insight meant to cut delays and prevent crashes.

The platform brings connected vehicle, infrastructure, freight, and safety data into one place. Its analytics measure intersection delay, systemwide travel time, emissions, and behavioral risk. Users can generate reports for corridors, intersections, before-after studies, or safety measures. One part of the system optimizes signal timing in real time to reduce delays and improve fuel efficiency. Another predicts crash risk, detects hazardous behavior, and recommends interventions.

The company announced that DDOT is expanding smart traffic signal monitoring across Washington, DC. That announcement says the expansion follows a pilot and reaches more than 1,600 signalized intersections citywide. An earlier announcement names Florida DOT District 5 and a real-time traffic management platform across 2,000 intersections.

before.name: Cyvl
before.description: Vehicle-mounted lidar + AI for pavement condition, sidewalk ADA, and street asset inventories - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026

paragraphs: Cyvl sells a sensor and software platform that shows cities what needs attention across every street, sidewalk and asset. Counties are a second audience, using it to keep sprawling road networks current.

A city team mounts the LiDAR and 360 degree imaging rig on a vehicle it already owns, and the drive itself does the collecting. Each drive becomes pavement scores, asset inventories and a ranked list of needs. The results live in one shared platform for public works, city leaders and residents. Coverage reaches past pavement to sidewalks and curb ramps assessed for an ADA baseline.

Cities and towns are described as capturing their entire right-of-way in a single pass. Counties are described as using the record to hold developers and utilities accountable for the condition they leave roads in. The company says Atlanta moved downtown pavement from 64 to 75, from fair to good, while potholes fell 60 percent.

before.name: Ecopia AI
before.description: AI-extracted road, sidewalk and asset basemaps for government agencies

paragraphs: Ecopia AI uses artificial intelligence to convert high-resolution geospatial imagery into accurate, up-to-date vector maps for data-driven decision-making. For municipal and state government the data is offered for transportation networks, public safety and stormwater planning. Off-the-shelf offerings sit alongside customized global feature extraction.

Its 3D Land Cover product delivers planimetric vector layers for buildings, roads, driveways, sidewalks, water bodies, sports fields and overlapping tree canopy, with height attribution for buildings. The company states that features are extracted from high-resolution imagery with greater than 95% geometric accuracy. Partner imagery providers capture fresh imagery every year, which lets the company detect change and deliver annual updates. A separate transportation product covers sidewalks, crosswalks, medians, bike lanes, turning lanes, paint striping and intersections. Those layers carry attributes such as width, material and feature type, distinguishing a left turn lane from a right turn lane.

The transportation data is aimed at AEC firms, MPOs and DOTs. Stated uses include assessing sidewalk width and curb characteristics against ADA regulations. Another stated use is emergency services and dispatch planning, drawing on 3D maps of buildings, roads and driveways. Ecopia says it produces millions of square kilometers of vector data per month. It also announced a self-serve platform for high-precision geospatial data downloads.

before.description: Solar road-weather stations and AI forecasting for municipal winter operations - exhibited at ASBO School Business 2026

paragraphs: Frost Solutions sells road weather monitoring hardware and software for the crews who fight snow and ice. The stated audience is municipalities and contractors.

The core device is a solar-powered unit that mounts easily and captures hyperlocal weather data every minute. It tracks road surface temperature, grip and coefficient of friction forecasts, air conditions and visibility. Site-level readings also cover pavement temperature, humidity, dew point and frost. The software reviews site photos and weather data every minute and raises an alert when conditions change. Its dashboard carries snow and frost alerts, surface temperature updates and hyperlocal 72-hour forecasts.

Contractors are told to put units in customer parking lots to decide where to send crews first. School districts are another named market, where campuses and multiple buildings are hard to cover. The site says it serves communities in 37 states and 7 provinces.

before.name: SWARCO
before.description: Traffic signals, controllers and ITS hardware/software to public road agencies

paragraphs: SWARCO supplies road marking systems, traffic technology and industrial glass products to the people who build and operate roads. The group is headquartered in Wattens near Innsbruck, Austria, and runs an international network of plants, offices and partners. Its portfolio reaches across road marking, signage, urban traffic management, parking, highway and tunnel management, public transport and street lighting.

For cycling infrastructure the company offers coloured area markings, using green for general lanes and red to flag spots where the risk is higher. Pictograms are made from preformed thermoplastics so they sit in a rider's line of sight. Choosing a system means weighing location, traffic intensity, cost and environmental compatibility. A separate line covers runways, taxiways and aprons, where markings have to hold up against fuels, deicers, engine oils and hydraulic fluids.

Airfield marking systems have been tested and approved by the German Federal Institute for Material Research and Testing. Airport paints and marking products are made in compliance with FAA and Federal specifications as well as EASA. The company counts 5,300 transportation experts and traces its outlook to founder Manfred Swarovski.

paragraphs: ExeVision sells project development software for road and highway work to state and local transportation agencies. Offerings are split between state agency and local agency needs, including software for county road construction.

before.name: CITYROVER
before.description: AI dashcams (EDGE/PULSE) for automated pothole and road-defect detection for public works - exhibited at CTAA EXPO 2026, APTA 2026

paragraphs: CITYROVER sells smart cameras and software that governments mount in vehicles already driving their streets, so road problems get spotted without a dedicated inspection trip. The stated aim is taking over inspection work that agencies would otherwise do by hand.

Detection happens on the camera itself, which uploads what it finds to the cloud for review. Staff get notifications carrying the location and images of the issue. The camera picks out potholes, manholes, dumped garbage, transit infrastructure problems and signs. Two other families sit beside it: PULSE for pavement rating, pavement markings and survey imagery, and COMPANION, an app for inspectors and work crews.

Government inspectors are the main users, reporting maintenance and operations issues automatically. An open API and off-the-shelf connectors move the data into systems an agency already runs. The site claims hundreds of governments as customers.

before.name: Dareesoft Inc.
before.description: On-vehicle AI that detects potholes and other road hazards in real time and feeds a road maintenance dashboard and API for city and state road authorities - exhibited at NACE 2026

paragraphs: Dareesoft sells road hazard detection that rides along in vehicles already using the road network. The offering is packaged as Road Information as a Service, an all-in-one solution for road maintenance. The company describes itself as an integrated road data company.

A device in the vehicle analyzes the road and transmits hazards to a cloud platform instantly. Each detection carries a high quality image with GPS coordinates, road network, timestamps and object size. Detected hazards appear on a road monitoring dashboard for remote inspection. An API suite lets the hazard data flow into systems an agency already runs.

Dareesoft was founded in 2020. Its company timeline lists a contract for the Seoul Metropolitan Government video-based pothole detection project. The same timeline records a project secured with Brazoria County, Texas. Another entry lists a project contract signed with New York City for speed signage. It also lists a Series B raise of KRW 4 billion.

before.name: Global Traffic Technologies (GTT)
before.description: Opticom emergency vehicle preemption and transit signal priority for cities

paragraphs: The business sells a traffic signal priority control platform, marketed as Opticom, to cities that want essential vehicles moving through intersections without delay. It covers two jobs: preemption that clears a path for fire, police and ambulance crews, and signal priority that keeps buses and light rail closer to schedule.

Whichever communication method a city uses, the steps are the same. When a crew activates lights and siren, equipment on the vehicle sends a request ahead to equipped intersections, which then sequence the lights to green on the approach being used. As soon as the vehicle is through, the intersection goes back to its normal cycle. Agencies can run cloud, satellite positioning and infrared deployments side by side rather than replacing everything at once.

The buyers are the people who run those services: fire and police leadership, ambulance directors, transit operations staff and fleet managers. The site dates the technology back close to six decades. Fleets can be connected through integrations with a number of vehicle and telematics vendors.

quote.text: Traffic signal priority and preemption solves this by giving the right vehicles a clear path at intersections so they arrive on time, safely, and on schedule.

before.name: Quarterhill
before.description: Tolling and intelligent transportation systems (owns IRD, ETC); acquiring Conduent's tolling unit

paragraphs: Quarterhill designs, develops, and deploys technology systems for the intelligent transportation systems industry, with a presence throughout North America and Europe. Its tolling work covers toll collection, and its safety and enforcement work covers commercial vehicle enforcement, freight compliance, and active transportation management. Multi modal solutions cover container tracking and port planning, border crossings, and axle-load and track monitoring on rail lines and highway corridors.

Rail products built on Sensor Line fiber optic sensors cover speed measurement, weigh in motion, flat wheel detection, track bed analysis, axle and wagon counting, and vibration analysis. These sensors are used for predictive maintenance and for detecting changes to track and rolling stock.

before.name: Diversified Computer Services (DCS)
before.description: CIMS work order, asset and daily task management software for county road, highway and public works departments - exhibited at NACE 2026

paragraphs: Diversified Computer Services sells information management software used by local governments to run daily operations. Its main product for that market is CIMS, which offers more than 25 functional modules for local government departments. The company says it has been helping local governments capture and manage information for more than 30 years.

CIMS centralizes and automates the creation, assignment, and tracking of tasks, projects, and work orders. Every functional module is made available to all customers, so enhancements reach the whole user community. Integrated mapping generates interactive maps based on Google Maps without specialist operators. More than 500 dynamic reports let departments measure performance and study trends. In the field, problems can be reported and converted into work orders, with GPS coordinates captured and photos uploaded.

Alongside CIMS the company sells TracSpot, GPS tracking software used by businesses and local governments for situational awareness. A facilities management system tracks work orders start to finish and shows where funds go through budget and purchase tracking. Ongoing training and support come with the standard subscription. Customers also get an invitation to an annual user conference.

paragraphs: BusPatrol runs school bus stop-arm enforcement programs alongside school districts, municipalities, and law enforcement agencies. The company says communities can enforce the law around stopped buses at no upfront cost.

before.name: Compass IoT
before.description: Connected-vehicle road safety and network analytics for road authorities - exhibited at ITS America 2026

paragraphs: Compass IoT sells connected vehicle data for road networks, taken from the cars themselves rather than roadside equipment or phones. The company says more than 3,000 users globally use its connected vehicle data to understand traffic across their road networks. Its Road Intelligence platform presents that network-wide vehicle data in a browser.

The data comes from cloud-connected vehicles that have an internet connection. Compass says it receives over a billion connected vehicle data points every day from 64 different car manufacturers. Each record can carry location, timestamp, speed, acceleration, make and model, plus road attributes such as the speed limit and pavement type. Coverage runs across virtually every road in Australia.

Published case studies show clients using the tools for road safety, city planning, and infrastructure questions. One covers Sunshine Coast Council measuring how speed cushions retrofitted at a pedestrian crossing changed driver behaviour. Afterwards, average speed in both directions dropped to 22km/h. Another describes the Inner West Council using data-driven evidence to lower speed limits for pedestrian and cyclist safety. Compass IoT UK has received funding from EIT Urban Mobility as part of the third SME Expansion Open Call.

before.name: Blyncsy
before.description: AI detection of pavement markings and road defects from crowdsourced dashcams (Bentley Systems) - exhibited at ITS America 2026

paragraphs: Blyncsy helps cities and state departments of transportation automate their roadway maintenance and asset inventory activities. Rather than sending crews out to look, it works from crowd-sourced dash camera imagery.

Machine learning algorithms and image processing applied to that imagery detect where and when pavement needs maintenance. Condition assessments run from pot holes to paint striping and crosswalk conditions. Paint lines are rated from 1, the worst, to 5, the best. In construction zones the same imagery detects work zone equipment to put those zones on the map. Those detections can also check whether a maintenance of traffic plan matches reality. A further model detects the presence of debris on and beside the road. The AI also estimates the size of the debris it finds.

Results are delivered directly into OpenGIS or another preferred platform. The company claims savings of up to 90% compared to traditional manual inspections. It puts the cost at $10 per centerline mile against $200 or more for a LiDAR scan. News items on the site include a City of Fort Worth partnership on the first phase of automated asset inventory. Another announces a sustainability partner designation in the Google Cloud Partner Advantage Program.

before.name: Applied Information
before.description: Connected-vehicle ITS and the Glance smart-city platform: signal monitoring, preemption, school beacons - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026, APTA 2026, ITS America 2026

paragraphs: Applied Information makes traffic technology that turns intersections, school zones and connected vehicles into one real-time system. The customers are cities, which manage their traffic and ITS assets through a web-based application called Glance.

Glance monitors intersection cabinet equipment, reporting AC power, battery back up, cabinet flash, stop time, conflict monitor status, door switches, fan status and vehicle detectors. For emergency vehicles, an in-vehicle unit uses a cellular signal to tell the system a route has started. The system works out the route and talks wirelessly to the traffic cabinet to clear traffic ahead of the vehicle. School beacon flashers and their schedules can be viewed and controlled from anywhere. A connected vehicle product communicates over C-V2X, 4G LTE cellular and 900MHz.

The company states its hardware is designed, assembled and tested in Alpharetta, Georgia, with components meeting domestic content thresholds. A connected school bus system warns drivers approaching an active school safety zone or exceeding the speed limit. A smartphone app, Glance TravelSafely, extends the technology to residents.

quote.text: The drivers know they’ve got a green light in front of them, they know that everyone else has a red light, and they know the traffic is going to move ahead of them.

paragraphs: Motive sells fleet software and hardware as one integrated suite built around AI. The buyers are commercial fleets, which the company describes as ranging from five or ten vehicles up to companies running thousands of them.

On the safety side, cameras and AI flag more than twenty kinds of event on the road. High-confidence events go straight to managers, while a safety team reviews the low-confidence ones to remove false positives. Vehicle tracking uses real-time GPS with traffic updates and weather overlays for route planning. Compliance work such as electronic logs, driver qualification, IFTA and CSA sits in the same platform. Equipment monitoring shows what share of the time an asset is in use and how long it sits dormant. Telematics from various equipment manufacturers is centralized in a single platform.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

before.name: Collective Data

paragraphs: Collective Data sells configurable asset management software to government agencies and other organizations with heavy operational demands. Its fleet product covers preventative maintenance scheduling, work orders, inspections, inventory control, and shop management.

Maintenance is scheduled automatically, with work orders and alerts meant to cut downtime and extend vehicle lifespan. Inspection schedules can be set by date, mileage, or engine hours. Telematics, fuel systems, and other tools can feed into the same platform. Data access is controlled by user role, with a full audit trail of changes. Add-on modules include single sign-on that supports OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect. A replacement forecasting module was developed with APWA standards in mind, according to the company.

A separate quartermaster product is built for law enforcement and public safety agencies. It tracks where fixed assets are located, who has them, and when they are due back. Employee signatures are captured during the issuance process. The company says private companies and government agencies have used its software for more than 25 years.

before.name: Sawatch Labs
before.description: EV fleet transition analytics for city, county and state fleets

paragraphs: Sawatch Labs sells fleet electrification software that uses mile-by-mile predictive analytics to determine EV suitability, cost modeling, infrastructure planning, vehicle management, and emissions reporting. The inputs are individual vehicle telematics data, which fleet managers use as the foundation for making data-driven decisions. Since 2017 the company has supported fleets in all 50 states.

paragraphs: Jacobs is a global professional services company that delivers consulting and advisory, design and implementation work across infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, environmental and technology challenges. The sectors listed on these pages include transport across airports, rail, roads and maritime, water, buildings, power transmission and distribution, and land use planning. Building solutions cover the planning, design, delivery and operation of buildings, from strategy and planning through design, delivery, operations and reinvestment.

A digital and AI line combines artificial intelligence, digital advisory and enterprise software for organizations that plan, build and operate infrastructure. Intelligent O&M applies AI-driven analytics to wastewater and drinking water treatment plants, predicting failures and optimizing processes. Clients named on these pages include the Central Utah Water Conservancy District, which selected Jacobs for engineering services on the proposed Strawberry High Line Improvement Project. before.name: AtomAI Solutions
before.description: Atom asset/maintenance management and Coordinate ROW/project coordination (ex-SADA, ex-dotMaps)

paragraphs: AtomAI Solutions sells a suite of software that agencies use to manage assets, work orders, project and utility coordination, permitting, and safety. Its two flagship products are Atom, an asset and maintenance management platform, and Coordinate, formerly dotMaps, a right-of-way and project coordination tool used by state and local agencies across the country.

Work templates can be defined by each agency so that task structures, fields, and workflows match its own operational processes. Forms built inside the platform can include required fields, dropdowns, conditional logic, and photo or video uploads. Every work order records labor hours, equipment usage, and materials consumed, either automatically or through entry in the field. Templated reports are meant to meet compliance and reporting requirements from agencies such as the FHWA, FRA, and EPA.

The company began as an internal startup within SADA Systems Inc. The full team and product suite divested in early 2023 to form AtomAI Solutions, Inc. as an independent company. Since then it has expanded its offerings to include a permitting solution built specifically for state and local governments.

before.name: Fieldman
before.description: Field work order and asset management software for local governments and utilities running smart meter and infrastructure projects - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: Fieldman is an American software and services company that helps utility contractors and municipalities manage assets, jobs, work orders, and field projects. The platform is built for AMI projects, where spreadsheets and generic work order software break down. The site says contractors have run it on more than 200 AMI projects.

Assets and work orders load into a web portal where managers and dispatchers track, update, and search them. Project requirements become digital workflows built with branch logic, so technicians are guided step by step. Scheduling covers resident appointment booking, blackout dates, inventory, and assignment by technician availability. In the field, technicians capture photos, GPS locations, signatures, and meter readings. Collection keeps working even in areas without internet access.

Fieldman is family-owned, with no venture backing and no public trading. It started in 2019, when a founder set out to build management software for utility field service projects. The company says its founders personally set up the platform for a customer's field operations. Its published client stories come from utilities and contractors running field operations on the platform.

before.name: Azuga
before.description: GPS fleet tracking and driver safety telematics for SMB and government fleets (Bridgestone)

paragraphs: Azuga sells GPS fleet tracking and dual-facing dashcam software meant to keep vehicles, assets and drivers safe. The company argues that such software should improve safety and not only day-to-day operations. It pitches the product as simple to use, affordable, customizable, and easy to install.

The company frames the work as a four-part improvement process folded into daily fleet operations. Driver scoring is meant to show managers and drivers alike how safely they are driving. A mobile app included in the subscription gives administrators and drivers separate views. For tools and small equipment, Bluetooth beacons are picked up by the company's cellular asset trackers. One tracker can detect and report on fifty beacons at a time. Vehicles that leave the factory with built-in telematics can connect to the platform without aftermarket hardware.

Azuga says customers have relied on it since 2013 for GPS fleet tracking and asset tracking. Insurance companies use its telematics data to measure and price risk in commercial vehicle portfolios. The company also says it works with government agencies on how transportation taxes, emissions data and tolls are collected. States and municipalities, it states, use the data to understand traffic patterns and road surface conditions.

paragraphs: Azuga sells GPS fleet tracking and dual-facing dashcam software meant to keep vehicles, assets and drivers safe. The company argues that such software should improve safety and not only day-to-day operations. It pitches the product as simple to use, affordable, customizable, and easy to install.

The company frames the work as a four-part improvement process folded into daily fleet operations. Driver scoring is meant to show managers and drivers alike how safely they are driving. A mobile app included in the subscription gives administrators and drivers separate views. For tools and small equipment, Bluetooth beacons are picked up by the company's cellular asset trackers. One tracker can detect and report on fifty beacons at a time. Vehicles that leave the factory with built-in telematics can connect to the platform without aftermarket hardware.

Azuga says customers have relied on it since 2013 for GPS fleet tracking and asset tracking. Insurance companies use its telematics data to measure and price risk in commercial vehicle portfolios. The company also says it works with government agencies on how transportation taxes, emissions data and tolls are collected. States and municipalities, it states, use the data to understand traffic patterns and road surface conditions.

quote.text: Azuga also helps states and municipalities understand traffic patterns and road surface conditions to improve infrastructure planning and upkeep.

paragraphs: Geotab sells fleet management technology that commercial vehicle operators use to track vehicles and run their operations from one system. The company describes what it offers as an open platform for safe, sustainable and cost-effective mobility powered by AI and data intelligence. Video safety is part of the same package, with dash cameras feeding into the MyGeotab software.

The GO tracking device plugs into a vehicle's onboard diagnostics port. Once driving begins it records location, speed, engine idling and distance. Dash cam footage and alert data upload to the cloud so managers can review video later. An analytics layer standardizes data from every vehicle source and enriches it with context such as road conditions, driver history and maintenance records. Developers can extend the platform with sample code and custom add-in pages.

Police and first responders are among the industries the site lists. Geotab reports more than six million connected vehicles. It also claims 26 years of fleet expertise. The company states that the platform is backed by ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II certifications and that its AI aligns with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Support is described as staffed around the clock by experts who are in-market rather than offshored.

paragraphs: Aurigo Software sells capital program management software to government agencies that plan, build and maintain public infrastructure. It also serves facility owners in areas such as data centers, life sciences, manufacturing, and energy and utilities. The company's platform, Masterworks, brings planning, execution, financials, right of way and analytics together in one system.

On the delivery side it coordinates contracts, schedules, costs and field work so teams can hold to the original plan and keep a complete audit trail. Compliance, funding transparency and governance are meant to sit inside everyday work so public money stays accountable. Agencies can change forms, workflows, business rules and dashboards through configuration rather than code. An AI layer called Lumina supports decision-making with compliance and governance built in, and the company says every insight and recommendation it produces can be audited and traced.

Cities, counties, transit agencies and transportation departments across North America use the platform to manage capital programs, replace legacy systems and automate federal reimbursements. The company claims more than 300 customers and over 20 years of capital program expertise behind the product. It also says the software monitors project signals to catch cost, schedule and delivery risks before they turn critical.

paragraphs: Eptura sells software for running physical workplaces, facilities and assets, aimed at organizations that operate buildings and want one view of them. One app handles enterprise asset management for teams tracking and maintaining physical assets across facilities, fleets and field operations.

Other apps cover workplace experience and resource scheduling, letting teams plan their week and book space. before.description: Fleet, fuel, and enterprise asset management software for governments and universities (Volaris) - exhibited at NAFA I&E 2026, NRPA 2026

paragraphs: AssetWorks builds software, hardware and consulting services for organizations whose work centers on assets and infrastructure. The buyers run commercial fleets or public infrastructure and want to control operating costs.

The fleet system, FleetFocus, is a central platform for maintenance, asset lifecycle tracking, fueling and reporting. A companion product, FuelFocus, watches fuel levels and transactions in real time so discrepancies surface immediately. A mobile extension puts inventory and work order management in the hands of technicians and storekeepers. A Power BI connection supports custom dashboards, advanced reporting and lifecycle analytics on the same data.

The company puts its own history at more than 40 years and the home page counts over 1,000 organizations using the products. Listed offices include one in Berwyn, Pennsylvania and a San Antonio location for education facilities, real estate and planning software. Case studies describe a county internal services department managing roughly 20,000 vehicles. Another covers a regional public transit agency running a fleet of more than 427 active vehicles.

paragraphs: inLogic sells RFID asset tracking software for organizations looking to streamline their asset tracking process. The product is RFTrack, a software platform that leverages RFID to help improve asset visibility by enabling organizations to automate fixed asset inventories, locate assets, and track the movement of assets in real-time. Delivery is described as turnkey, covering software, readers, tags and implementation services alongside the platform itself.

The about page frames two uses: automating an annual fixed asset inventory audit, and providing real-time visibility of assets. The homepage describes a commercial off-the-shelf platform that helps automate the process of tracking fixed assets for Education, Government, Defense, Aerospace, Research, IT, and Data Center customers. The about page lists Education, Government, Defense, Aerospace, Research, Manufacturing, and other organizations as the users the platform helps save time, reduce operating costs, and improve fixed asset visibility.

The about page says the company was founded in 2001 with a focus on developing data collection solutions, that its focus transitioned to RFID in 2004, and that its first RFID-based product was released in 2005. RFID is a data collection technology that uses radio frequency communication to collect data from RFID tags, which can uniquely identify objects such as assets or people.

paragraphs: RTVision sells configurable cloud software for managing infrastructure work. The site groups that software for transportation, government, water and utilities, and consultants. Products named on the site cover construction project management, right of way, capital improvement planning, asset management, invoice management, time and attendance, and online permits.

The construction project management product provides agencies, consultants, and contractors with access to project information from early planning through inspections and payments. The permit product automates the permit process for both the applicant and the agency, in or out of the office. Case studies on the site describe county permitting, right-of-way and construction management, and capital program oversight for a regional wastewater district.

paragraphs: FASTER sells fleet management and asset maintenance software as one platform. The public sector is the core audience, built for municipalities, school systems, transit, and utilities.

Coverage runs from acquisition planning through disposal of an asset. Day to day, that means automated preventive maintenance scheduling, real-time parts tracking, and streamlined work orders. Managers track total cost of ownership, downtime, and utilization by vehicle, department, or fleet. A customer portal lets vehicle users request repairs online, view repair history, and manage appointments.

The company says more than 400 organizations manage over one million assets on FASTER across North America. Those customers include city governments, universities, utilities, public works departments, and private fleet operators. The site claims over 40 years of helping organizations run safer, smarter, and more efficiently. It describes itself as a US-based company with US-based product, engineering, and support teams. The homepage also lists SOC 2 compliant security and data protection. FASTER is part of Transit Technologies.

paragraphs: KloudGin sells work and asset management software to water and wastewater utilities. Gas utilities are a second market for the same platform. Municipalities and other public sector agencies are a third.

One part of the platform handles construction work management for complex projects, built on utility industry expertise. An enterprise asset management side unifies assets and workforce to optimize operations. Work management gives crews a view of assets, work orders, records and AI-native decision support. Prebuilt modules cover specific utility jobs such as automating fire hydrant maintenance. Others handle 811 ticket automation for dig requests. Another helps crews identify, document and replace lead service lines. GIS capabilities are embedded to support location-based customer service, and a separate adapter serves SAP customers.

An IDC MarketScape evaluation cited on the site names the company a Leader in utilities enterprise asset management. The company has announced a partnership with Black & Veatch. Its chief executive is named on the site as Vikram Takru. It also positions itself as a platform choice for cities.

paragraphs: Accruent sells software for managing buildings, spaces and physical assets across every stage of real estate, facilities and asset management. The stated aim is to run the full lifecycle of assets and facilities with connected workflows and reporting behind it.

One product, EMS, schedules meeting rooms, events, shared spaces, desks and exams. In higher education it supports self-service booking for classrooms, labs and campus events. A second product, FAMIS 360, centralizes maintenance, space planning and energy management for facility operations. Its modules track properties and locations down to floors, spaces and subspaces, along with occupancy and the work orders attached to them.

The home page claims more than 5,000 organizations worldwide as customers. Customer stories on the site lean toward higher education, including one on how the University of Missouri handled facility operations. For public agencies, the lease accounting product is presented as a way to stay in line with ASC 842, IFRS and GASB.
