before.name: Camis
before.description: Reservation and park operations systems for state, provincial and federal parks

paragraphs: Camis sells reservation and park management software to government-operated parks, marinas and harbors, work the company says it has done for more than 46 years. Visitors use it to book a camping trip, a day-use pass, a harbor stay or a ticketed event.

Bookings can come in ahead of time, at the gate, or through a call center. Payment runs through the same platform, whether the visitor is online or standing at a park office. A combined on-site and webstore system handles merchandise sales with real-time inventory tracking, and the company describes it as fully PCI and SOC compliant. Field staff get a separate enforcement app called Sidekick, built for the job assignments of wardens and rangers. On the back end, staff work from real-time data and customizable reports.

The company describes its origin as outdoor enthusiasts who saw a better way to connect people to parks. Its own timeline starts with a first park contract at Craigleith Provincial Park. The same timeline records that the business was acquired by Banyan Software. It also claims continued expansion across more than 30 national, provincial and state parks.

before.name: Better Impact
before.description: Volunteer management software for parks, libraries and government agencies - exhibited at Animal Care Expo 2026

paragraphs: Better Impact sells volunteer management software used by organizations to automate scheduling, track hours and communicate with volunteers. A membership product manages member profiles, automates renewals and supports engagement across the member lifecycle. A client product works alongside the volunteer system to coordinate volunteer and client interactions.

Coordinators get self-scheduling, automated communications, online training modules and one-click reports. The broader promise is streamlined scheduling, less administrative burden and hour tracking in one system. A separate offering called Volunteer Link is built for corporate social responsibility teams that want to engage employees, strengthen community partnerships and measure impact. It gives employees access to over 200,000 volunteer opportunities across the US and Canada. Reports come export-ready for ESG disclosures, board presentations and annual CSR summaries.

The company says more than 85,000 organizations use its software. Its published case studies include a hospice rethinking how it coordinates care. In March 2026 it announced the acquisition of Get Connected by Galaxy Digital, another volunteer management software provider. Leadership is listed as chief executive Houston Goodwin and president Tim Sarazen.

before.name: InitLive (Bloomerang Volunteer)
before.description: Event volunteer scheduling and check-in for festivals and public events

paragraphs: Bloomerang Volunteer is volunteer management software for nonprofits, covering recruiting, scheduling, engagement, tracking and reporting. It is aimed at organizations of any size, including those with large volunteer bases, recurring shifts and multiple sites or programs.

Scheduling filters volunteers by skills, roles, availability and interests to match them to open shifts. Volunteers use a mobile app to manage schedules, stay informed and check in on site. Background checks run inside the platform against an organization's own safety and compliance standards. Reporting turns volunteer hours into custom reports showing dollars saved through volunteer work. Because donors, volunteers and fundraising sit on one platform, volunteer data can be used to identify donor prospects.

The volunteer product arrived by acquisition, and the company milestone list records that Bloomerang acquired InitLive and launched Bloomerang Volunteer Management. Bloomerang presents itself as a unified giving platform built for purpose. The same page claims over ten years of purpose-built software. Other milestones include acquiring Qgiv to expand the giving platform.

before.name: Galaxy Digital
before.description: Get Connected volunteer management for municipalities and public agencies

paragraphs: Galaxy Digital sells volunteer management software under the Get Connected name, built for organizations that recruit, schedule, track and report on volunteers. The organizations described range from food banks and healthcare systems to municipal departments and corporate social impact teams.

The platform puts scheduling, hour tracking, communication and reporting in one place. Volunteers check in through an onsite kiosk or a free mobile app. Liability waivers and e-signatures are collected and stored digitally. The software is sold in tiers, with the largest aimed at organizations running multiple programs or locations under separate volunteer coordinators.

A separate edition called Center serves organizations that sit at the middle of a network of nonprofit partners. That edition adds statewide and citywide volunteerism reporting. The company states its network reaches 405 volunteer centers, more than 60,000 mission-driven organizations and millions of volunteers. It also reports acquiring HandsOn Connect.

before.name: Perry Weather
before.description: Weather safety platform: WBGT heat monitoring, lightning alerts, stations and sirens for parks and athletics - exhibited at NRPA 2026

paragraphs: Perry Weather sells a weather safety platform that pairs monitoring hardware at a customer site with automated alerting, so an entire staff works from the same reading of conditions. The buyers it names are schools, cities, golf clubs, and industrial firms.

Stations at the customer location measure heat stress, lightning, precipitation, wind, and air quality, refreshing every five minutes in the mobile app and dashboard. Each organization writes its own thresholds and decides who gets notified when one is crossed. Alerts can go to phones or to an outdoor siren system. Countdown timers mark the moment it is safe to resume play or work. All-clears go out automatically once the threat has passed.

Colin Perry founded the company in 2013. It reports more than 5,000 organizations nationwide as customers. It also counts over 200 million alerts sent, covering hazards from heat stress to lightning. Arthur Ventures led a $15M Series B. The stated markets run across athletics, golf, parks and recreation, energy, and airports.

paragraphs: DTN sells forecasting and risk planning for organizations whose operations turn on weather. Refined fuel markets are another line of business, with real-time visibility, pricing and supply chain intelligence.

The products are packaged as vertical hubs tailored to the workflows of a given sector. One is aimed at utilities, where the pitch is outage response and grid reliability. He arrived most recently from Spirent Communications, where he led global sales and services. DTN has also announced work on real-time weather intelligence using NVIDIA Earth-2 on AWS.

before.name: Baron Weather
before.description: Weather data, alerting and decision tools for government agencies - exhibited at IAEM 2026

paragraphs: Baron Weather sells weather data, forecasting and alerting tools to businesses, government agencies and communities. Its catalog holds hundreds of datasets, with information down to the street level. The company argues that free or incomplete sources leave organizations either over-prepared and wasteful or under-prepared and at risk.

Baron blends data from many sources into insights using analytical processes, machine learning, and AI. Many of its products carry built-in alerting and recommended actions to guide a decision. The company also builds weather radar hardware it describes as engineered for durability and sustainability. Its forecast modeling covers atmospheric, hydrological, marine, air quality, and road surface coupled models. Content is prepackaged so it can be shared quickly and understood without expertise.

The company traces its mission to 1989, when an F4 tornado devastated parts of Huntsville, Alabama. Its customer base spans government agencies, emergency managers, small startups, and Fortune 500 companies. Baron lists ISO 9001 quality management among the credentials behind its processes. ISO 14001 environmental management is listed as well.

paragraphs: Earth Networks sells hyperlocal weather intelligence and real-time lightning detection to organizations that have to make safety decisions outdoors. A core use is warning people who work and play outdoors when lightning is approaching.

The company frames the lightning network as detection rather than prediction. It claims coverage in more than 90 countries. Warnings reach people by email, text message and mobile push notification. Audible outdoor horns carry the same warning across a site. Its Sferic Maps product tracks more than 80 real-time weather conditions on a map. Sferic Connect lets administrators notify staff of dangerous weather on iOS and Android devices, and can stop end users from opting out.

Meteorological staff are on hand around the clock when a customer is unsure what to do. Product pages point at schools as one setting for the alerts. Airports are another. The company also publishes a report on lightning detected across the United States.

before.name: BECS Technology
before.description: BECSys pool chemistry automation controllers with cloud remote monitoring for municipal aquatic centers - exhibited at AB Show 2026

paragraphs: BECS Technology builds electronic controllers, starting with water chemistry and filtration controls used on swimming pools, water parks, spas and splash pads. A second line goes into pork and poultry barns, where the company says its products help assure livestock health. A third covers refrigeration, with controls that supermarkets, convenience stores and liquor stores use to hold groceries at temperature.

A water chemistry controller watches the pool continuously and decides when the water needs attention. Operators reach those controllers through an online service the company describes as simple and secure. On the livestock side, the systems track feed inventory across a farm and send real-time data back to feed mills.

The company was incorporated in 1991. Its original ownership group has remained unchanged and has been together for over 30 years. More than 50,000 controllers have been designed and manufactured over that period. All manufacturing is performed onsite at a facility in Saint Louis, Missouri. The BECSys line of water treatment controllers was introduced in 2005. Before that, many products were marketed and distributed under the names of partner organizations.

before.name: Pronesis
before.description: AI-powered movement assessment platform - exhibited at AB Show 2026

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "© 2026 Pronesis. A MedVanta Company. All rights reserved." Fetched https://mypronesis.com. Live and matches the description 'AI-powered movement assessment platform': the site sells 'AI-driven 3D motion analysis to prevent injuries, optimize performance, and deliver personalized exercise programs for athletes, employers, military, and seniors.' Rule 3 checked carefully because Pronesis is a subsidiary brand ('Pronesis - A MedVanta Company'): mypronesis.com is Pronesis's OWN standalone site, not the parent MedVanta's corporate domain, so this is the correct record and does not risk importing MedVanta's postings. CAVEAT for board fit, flagging rather than rejecting since the description does match: I found NO evidence Pronesis sells to state or local government. Its four stated markets are athletes/trainers/gyms, employers, military, and aging adults/seniors - military is federal, and the rest are commercial or healthcare. No police, fire, public safety or municipal customers appear anywhere on the site. Also note the site has no careers/jobs link of its own, so hiring likely runs through MedVanta - worth checking before the board treats this as a scrapable source.

before.name: CampMinder
before.description: Camp management and registration software for camps including municipal programs

paragraphs: Campminder makes management software for summer camps of every shape, from day camps to sleepaway programs and from twenty campers to two thousand. It is sold by role, with separate material pitched to camp owners and directors and to registrars and administrators.

Families register from their own devices, and the forms they fill out land in one organized place. Payments are collected and tracked inside the enrollment hub. A transportation planner lets staff drag and drop buses, routes, schedules and shuttles. Messaging tools pull camp data to send specific emails and texts to campers, parents, staff and alumni. An API distributes report data instantly to other departments. A companion app gives parents a photo feed that finds their child using facial recognition.

The company describes itself as a customer-centric business 22 years strong. Both product suites are tiered on the number of enrolled campers in the camp. Onboarding covers website integrations, historic data import and merchant account setup in fewer than three weeks. Camps across North America are described as using the platform to coordinate the logistics of running their programs.

before.name: CampDoc
before.description: Camp management software with electronic health records for camps, schools, and youth programs - exhibited at NRPA 2026

paragraphs: CampDoc sells camp and youth program software built for registration, health management, and day-to-day operations. The buyers are organizations that run programs for children and students, and the company says it powers more than 1,250 camps, youth programs and school programs. Signups, payments, rosters and family-facing workflows sit in one place.

On the health side, staff collect health forms, manage medications, document incidents, and keep records accessible when they need them. The health forms are digital and use conditional logic. Medication administration runs through an eMAR. Attendance, communication, reporting and daily program operations are kept together in one place. Rosters and health records stay aligned across the system.

For IT and compliance reviewers, the company points to SOC 2 Type II controls, role-based access to PHI, single sign-on for organizations that require it, and multi-factor authentication. It also states that the platform is HIPAA and FERPA compliant. Plans start at $355 per month. Onboarding, training, support and compliance are included in every plan, according to the pricing section. Published customer stories include a municipal parks and recreation department that replaced paper forms and manual tracking.

before.name: Arly
before.description: AI-embedded youth program management (enrollment, payments, safety) from nonprofit BellXcel - exhibited at NRPA 2026

paragraphs: Arly is youth program management software that puts every layer of program operations in one platform. The people who buy it run programs for children, handling enrollment, pricing and payments in the same place.

Families sign up through a customized portal with one log-in, completing forms and uploading documents. Billing and account processing sit alongside, with revenue tracked in real time. Participants are grouped and staff assigned to them for attendance taking and access to health and safety information. Check-in and check-out verifies authorized pick-up contacts in real time. An assistant called Arly Compass is described as part of the platform itself.

Curriculum is sold alongside the software, one set of it created in partnership with Scholastic. A summer package runs five to six weeks of ninety-minute daily instruction in reading, writing and math. Testimonials on the site are attributed to program staff at YMCA organizations, including the YMCA of Central Virginia. Staff onboarding includes self-paced learning and support from the company's customer experience team.

before.name: Labrie Group
before.description: Refuse and recycling collection vehicles for municipalities across North America

paragraphs: Labrie Group designs and manufactures waste collection vehicles for the solid waste industry in North America. The trucks are sold under the Labrie, Leach, and Wittke brands. Since 1971 the company has distributed and supported those products through a distributor network spanning the United States and Canada.

Their clientele ranges from private entrepreneurs in the waste hauling sector to national waste management service providers. The customer base also counts hundreds of small towns and counties, as well as major municipalities and cities. The company describes servicing millions of citizens in cities and municipalities all over North America.

Labrie Group supports over 30 distributors across the United States and Canada, and those distributors have over 50 individual locations across North America. Maintenance, repairs, and retrofits are handled by technicians in St-Romuald, Quebec, CA, and Lafayette, GA, USA. Labrie Environmental Group is part of Hiab.

before.name: Enevo
before.description: Waste fill-level sensors and monitoring analytics for municipal and commercial collection

paragraphs: Enevo sells waste container sensors and a cloud software platform to haulers, waste services companies, property managers, cities and campuses that want a clearer picture of their waste operations. The stated point of collecting that data is to let an operator control collection better and improve recycling rates.

Sensors report hourly fill levels and collection events, and the platform turns those readings into trends showing when a container needs picking up. An alert system flags sudden build ups and unforeseen events such as theft, fire or vandalism. A routing engine and scheduler compares service needs against available truck resources and proposes changes based on fill level trends and seasonal variation. Drivers work from an app built around routing, navigation and reporting. Historical fill and collection data can be pulled into other systems through a REST API.

The company says it was founded in 2010 by veterans of the wireless and telecom industry. Its customers run from small regional recyclers to large national waste management companies. Enevo also names property managers, cities, municipalities and higher education and corporate campuses among the groups whose waste data needs it serves.

paragraphs: Bigbelly sells enclosed trash and recycling bins to towns, business improvement districts, and large cities. Compacting models are stated to hold five times the capacity of traditional bins, meaning fewer collections.

Fullness-indicating and smart bins are meant to eliminate overflows and tell crews when and where to collect. Connected Smart and Smart Max bins communicate ready-to-collect status. The municipal page describes the City of Philadelphia decreasing collection frequency from 17 times to just 3 times per week. The airports page describes Copenhagen Airport introducing 64 Bigbelly bins and CLEAN cloud-based software. Amusement parks and zoos are another stated market.

before.name: Greyparrot
before.description: AI waste-recognition cameras and analytics for sorting plants

paragraphs: Greyparrot turns the waste passing through materials recovery facilities into data, serving both the teams that sort materials and the brands that design them. Its main product, Analyzer, is a process optimisation tool giving recyclers and waste sorting facilities continuous AI waste analytics across every sorting line.

Camera units above conveyor belts identify materials continuously, generating a real-time stream of composition, throughput and purity data across every monitored line. That data feeds a portal that organises it into four interlinked dashboards. Staff can review composition down to the minute and replay actual line images to identify where and when issues happened. A second product, Sync, connects Analyzer data into operational control systems and business reporting environments.

The practice this displaces, manual sampling, ties up operator hours and covers less than 0.1% of throughput. The company lists 250+ Analyzer units active. The same page states ISO 27001 and Cyber Essentials. One named user is KSI Recycling, described as one of the largest recyclers in the Netherlands, which did not deploy the portal all at once. A press item listed on the homepage reports a $27M Series B raise.

paragraphs: Curbtender builds refuse collection trucks and claims over 50 years of experience manufacturing automated side loaders. Design and manufacturing happen in Cedar Falls, Iowa and Gothenburg, Nebraska.

The company produces 13 different refuse truck models. The original Curbtender is described as the first commercially produced automated side loader in the United States waste industry. That flagship was renamed the PowerPak in 2017. Manual side loading refuse products are built as well. Rear loaders come in a full range of body sizes and performance packages, and two front loader models round out the range. On the automated side loaders, the lift arm can raise up to 2,000 pounds and comes with a standard five year structural warranty.

The assets of Wayne Industrial Holdings were purchased in 2017, when Kevin Watje was named chief executive. Curbtender Sweepers is a wholly owned subsidiary, covering grapple loaders, leaf and litter vacuums and street sweepers. The company has begun integrating its products with all electric truck chassis platforms.

before.name: Routeware
before.description: Routing, in-cab fleet tech, and resident apps for waste operations - exhibited at SWANA WASTECON 2025

paragraphs: Routeware sells digital technology for waste, recycling and heavy-duty fleet operations. The buyers are private haulers and municipal fleets. The software pulls collection, customer and business operations into one place.

Its routing product lets staff densify and edit routes and optimize entire fleets. Routes can be updated and stops reassigned in real time, with automatic sequencing. Dispatch gives a single view of orders, resources, status and inventory. Helper routes are built by drag and drop and resequenced on the spot. The back-office dispatch system is tied to the on-board computers in the truck.

The company describes the setup as hardware-light and cloud-based. It lists integrations with AWS, Esri, Geotab and Samsara. Some customers run several heavy-duty fleets, including snowplows and sweeper trucks. A separate product handles medical waste from end to end. Another is recycling software built around California mandates. The company says it has worked on digital transformation in waste and recycling for over twenty years.

before.name: Waste Robotics
before.description: Robotic sorting systems for organics and recycling plants serving municipalities

paragraphs: Waste Robotics builds AI-powered sorting robots for the waste stream. Its customers are recycling facilities, and the company frames the goal as safer and more efficient operations.

One line of robots is aimed at construction and demolition waste, picking out and separating materials such as wood, concrete and stone. Those machines are specified to run around the clock, destack materials, lift up to 20 kg, and carry an intelligent gripper. A hyperspectral camera lets the system tell one type of wood from another. A second configuration works on pre-sorting lines, pulling bulky items off the belt before they can damage equipment. The company says those bag-sorting robots are running in many cities across France on co-collection programs.

The site lists a Montreal address among its locations. Its chief executive is described as bringing deployment experience across audio-digital software, renewable energy and waste management. before.name: CP Group
before.description: Recycling equipment and turnkey MRF systems for municipal waste programs

paragraphs: CP Group designs, manufactures, installs, and services sorting machinery for the waste and recycling industry. It sells turnkey systems for both new material recovery facilities and retrofits of existing ones. A project management team handles third parties, scheduling, shipping, and installation.

Designing a facility begins with collaborative design meetings, cost reviews, and civil and electrical considerations. The equipment itself is engineered and manufactured in the United States. The shop has 115,000 sq. ft. of manufacturing space and 435,600 sq. ft. of storage on 9 acres. At startup and commissioning, the team goes over compliance, operations, and safety with the customer. Support afterward covers spare parts, process upgrades, and troubleshooting.

The company dates its machinery to the invention of the first commercial aluminum can flattener in 1977, and its name to Can Pac. It later acquired Krause Manufacturing, which makes construction and demolition separation equipment, and Advanced MRF, a specialist in intelligent motor controls and data acquisition. It says it owned and operated a material recovery facility for over 25 years, processing half of the city of San Diego's curbside recycling. That adds up to nearly 50 years of hands-on experience by its own account.

before.description: ArcGIS route optimization for waste/recycling collection and postal/utility fleets (FedEx-owned, 2025) - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, SWANA WASTECON 2025

paragraphs: RouteSmart Technologies sells software that plans and optimizes vehicle routes for service and delivery fleets. Its routing solutions are sold for newspaper, postal and parcel, public works, and utilities operations. Waste collection work is split into residential, commercial, and roll-off routing, and the same solutions cover street sweeping, snow removal, work orders and inspections.

The software is built on Esri mapping products, and RouteSmart for ArcGIS connects the routing algorithms to that platform. Clients can also reach the solvers through a hosted environment under the name Routing-as-a-Service. FedEx acquired RouteSmart Technologies.

Named clients include the U.S. Postal Service, for which letter carrier route planning began through Electronic Data Systems. A roll-off waste solution serves commercial and municipal Public Works clients. Other named clients are Southern California Gas Company in utilities and, in newspaper distribution, the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times.

paragraphs: Emerge Knowledge sells Re-TRAC, a cloud-based platform for collecting, managing, and reporting materials management data. The company presents it as a suite meant to centralize reporting, simplify data management, and improve data quality.

One module pulls together data from landfills, material recovery facilities, transfer stations, and composting facilities in a single place. A hauler reporting module centralizes the permit application process, tracks pick-ups, monitors collection costs, and calculates greenhouse gas emissions. Another is aimed at grantmaking and other funding initiatives. A further module is described as reducing the administrative burden of monitoring compliance with commercial, multi-family, and construction and demolition recycling ordinances.

Several of these solutions are listed as a best fit for counties and regional government agencies. The company states that Re-TRAC is SOC 2 Type II compliant. It also claims decades of experience in this field. Buyers whose needs fall outside the packaged modules are invited to schedule a free consultation to design something tailored to their own data collection needs.

paragraphs: EverestLabs sells vision AI, software agents and robotics meant to digitize and automate material processing plants. The company frames the work as transforming recycled and virgin material processing. Its stated buyers are operators in recycling, resource recovery, metals, e-waste, packaging, and mining.

The software side, Navigator, is described as a vision and agentic AI platform that gives every operator a process engineer, an equipment expert, and a data analyst in one chat. EverestLabs states that Navigator never acts autonomously. Equipment presets are applied only once an operator approves them. On the hardware side, the robotic sorting cell has a compact 3x3 ft footprint and works over existing conveyor belts without expensive retrofit. Those cells are presented as fully turnkey and remotely managed, delivered by a 24/7 staffed Remote Operations Center.

The company says its vision system covers 65 or more material classes at over 95% detection accuracy. On commercial terms, the site says payback lands in under 12 months, guaranteed by SLA. EverestLabs is headquartered in Fremont, California.

before.name: GreenQ
before.description: Truck-mounted sensors weighing and analyzing household waste for municipalities

paragraphs: GreenQ sells equipment and software that turn an ordinary garbage truck into an instrumented one. The company says it designs the technology for municipalities, collection vendors, and system integrators.

A tracking device is installed on the truck, where it weighs incoming garbage and tracks route and mileage. Because the hardware sits on the truck, no sensors need to be added to the bins. A recommendations engine then suggests logistical improvements and route optimization from the aggregated data. Results reach users through a dashboard of reports and analytics. The same approach extends to grapple trucks, where mounting the system measures bulk waste and monitors collection.

The company was established in 2015 with a stated goal of bringing efficient technology to waste management. Its stated aim is that municipalities can reduce expenses, reduce emissions, and provide better services to their citizens. One case study reports a city of 120,000 residents cutting costs and emissions by over 50 percent. Another describes launching the real-time monitoring and analytics platform in an IBM Bluemix environment on serverless IBM Cloud Functions.

paragraphs: Ecube Labs sells waste management systems pitched at cities that want cleaner streets and lower collection costs. The company was established in 2011. Buyers are cities and waste collection organizations trying to cut costs by dropping unnecessary pickups and running dynamic routes and schedules.

The method is an integrated IoT-based system that the company says dramatically improves the efficiency of waste collection. On the street side, the bins draw on the sun to compact what they hold. The claim made on the home page is an improvement in collection efficiency of 50% or more. Fewer pickups are also tied to public cleanliness, by reducing the impact of overflowing bins.

The company keeps offices in North America and Asia. It says its products and services can be seen across North and South America, Europe and the Middle East. For public buyers, the site says members can acquire the products and services without going through the request for proposal process. Prospects elsewhere are pointed toward a local distributor.

The company says it reaches millions of people and provides services to waste companies, smart cities and municipalities. Its about page counts more than 10,000 users, three or more global offices, and over 40 countries.

before.name: AMP
before.description: AI robotic sorting systems for recycling facilities (MRFs) - exhibited at SWANA WASTECON 2025, WasteExpo 2027

paragraphs: AMP designs, builds, and operates facilities that sort single-stream recycling and municipal solid waste using artificial intelligence. The buyers are waste companies and municipalities, offered sortation services and automation at scale.

The facility product, AMP ONE, is a fully automated sorting plant. It takes in single stream material, municipal solid waste, plant residue and mixed plastics and turns them into bales. Dozens of jet sorters and cameras characterize the stream continuously as it passes. Each finished bale is tagged with a bar code linked to the composition and purity of the material inside it.

For municipal solid waste, AMP states that it operates the facility itself and charges a per-ton processing rate with guaranteed diversion. The company puts typical diversion above 60 percent. It says custom plants can be operational in less than a year. Recovery of target materials is put at more than 90 percent.

quote.text: AMP ONE recovers 90%+ of target materials without touching a human hand.

before.name: 3rd Eye
before.description: Camera and telematics systems for refuse fleets used by municipal sanitation departments - exhibited at WasteExpo 2027

paragraphs: 3rd Eye sells modular, subscription-based software that runs on top of its own heavy-duty truck camera systems. Its buyers are waste hauling companies that have to manage collection fleets safely and stay connected to their customers. A truck can carry up to eight cameras for a full view around the vehicle.

Video and telematics data upload to the cloud, where they become safety events that a review team turns into driver coaching material. A maintenance module watches the chassis, body and equipment continuously. It hands mechanics a list of repairs ranked by severity or by how long remains before failure. Other modules take on tax paperwork, recording the data behind IFTA reporting and excise fuel tax recovery.

Contamination detection spots recycling contamination and other non-conforming refuse at the point of collection. Adding the route review module helps haulers plan and report the annual reviews that California State Bill 1383 requires. Container quality reviews photograph and geolocate each collection event to find carts needing repair or replacement. The company presents itself as part of Environmental Solutions Group alongside Soft-Pak and Heil, under the Connected Collections banner. Equipment can be taken monthly rather than bought outright, on what the company calls a Hardware as a Service model.

paragraphs: Sensoneo sells end-to-end solutions for data-driven waste management and a digitalised circular economy. Its ultrasonic bin sensor product line is offered to get control of waste fill-levels in bins, dumpsters and containers. before.name: Glacier
before.description: AI recycling-sorting robots and real-time bale/line data

paragraphs: Glacier makes sorting robots for recycling plants, pairing computer vision with mechanical picking to pull more material off the line. The company sells to two audiences at once: the material recovery facilities that run those lines, and consumer brands that want to know what becomes of their packaging.

The robots are compact and built to recover plastics, film and flexibles, paper, OCC, and metals. Behind the picking sit vision models the company says were trained on billions of real recycling images. Operators follow the results on dashboards that report down to the individual item.

Glacier says its robots are built specifically for material recovery facilities, with AI giving visibility at the item level. The company frames its purpose as a world where nothing valuable ends up in a landfill. It also says the team is growing and that it is hiring across engineering, operations, and field support.

before.name: Recycle Coach
before.description: Resident-facing recycling education and collection reminder apps for municipalities - exhibited at SWANA WASTECON 2025

paragraphs: Recycle Coach sells mobile and web app technology that municipalities use to give residents local waste and recycling information. The company describes its offering as custom waste and recycling solutions for cities, haulers, and organizations. Alongside the resident app, a Client Portal lets staff edit disposal requirements and send reminder messages. Analytics show which materials residents are searching for and where they need help, which the pages position as input to outreach campaigns.

The about page dates the business to 2001, when it began with wall recycling calendars for municipalities without extra budget for education. A decade later it launched a mobile app for local waste and recycling programs called My Waste. The same page states that the company now supports 1,700+ municipalities and millions of people.

Through the partnerships page, the same technology is offered white labeled, with a customizable web app adapted to a partner brand identity. That page also describes integration with digital 311 software so resident submissions about missed pick-ups or broken carts can be routed to the right teams. Beyond municipal programs, the pages describe a workplace product for teaching employees how to dispose of items in the office.

quote.text: With more than two decades in the waste and recycling industry, our mission remains the same: to help all organizations modernize communication and better their communities.

provenance.quote: Reach your residents wherever they are and put trusted information at their fingertips through our mobile and web app technology.
Custom waste & recycling solutions for cities, haulers, and organizations
From editing disposal requirements to sending out reminder messages, keeping your residents informed has never been easier with the help of our intuitive Client Portal.
See which materials residents are searching for, how they’re engaging, and where they need a little bit of help.

We began our journey in 2001 helping communities educate residents through traditional wall recycling calendars, an inexpensive solution for municipalities that didn’t have extra budget for education.

before.name: Heil Environmental
before.description: Refuse collection truck bodies sold to municipal sanitation fleets

paragraphs: Heil designs and manufactures the bodies that go on garbage trucks, selling to the fleets that collect refuse. The range runs from front loaders and automated front loaders to rear loaders, automated side loaders, and multi-compartment rear loaders.

The bodies are made in the United States, at a plant in Fort Payne, Alabama, that the company calls home. The product the site leads with is the RevAMP, a fully electric automated side loader. It is described as running with an auger compactor and no hydraulics on route. A training programme called Nexteligence is built for service technicians working on the Heil product line.

The company dates itself to 1901 and says it has built its reputation in the solid waste industry since then. It began as the Heil Railjoint Welding Company, founded by Julius P. Heil. Heil was later acquired and became a subsidiary within Dover Corporation. Dover then combined Heil Environmental, Marathon Equipment Company, and Bayne Machine Works into Environmental Solutions Group. Terex Corporation acquired Environmental Solutions Group on October 8, 2024.
